items.title: Imágenes Vevey: Familias, Te amo
items.content:
¡Familias, te odio! , tronó André Gide en 1897, en Frutas de la TierraMás de un siglo más tarde, en la orilla del lago de Ginebra, el sentimiento ha volteado. Familias, te amo, entonces, y configurado en música: para la décima edición de la bienal que fundó en 2008, Stefano Stoll sacó su tema de la Hermana Sledge, “Somos familia”, la banda sonora obligatoria de bodas y bautismos, que entró en el Grammy Hall of Fame el mismo año que nació Imágenes Vevey (fate tiene sentido de la boda).

Los visitantes que salen del tren son encontrados inmediatamente por un rostro familiar. En la Place de la Gare, Martin Parr se sienta entre las flores, mientras que detrás de él Alice, la hija de Siân Davey, ondea un globo. El fotógrafo inglés, que murió en diciembre de 2025, aparece en la serie “El jardín”, Siân Davey sobre un jardín salvaje abierto a los vecinos, seres queridos y transeúntes.

En el Grande Place, entre el Grenette y el Bois d’Amour, Barbara Davatz unfurls an open-air family tree. Una obra maestra de paciencia. En 1982, en un Zurich todavía electrificado por disturbios juveniles, el fotógrafo suizo, nacido en 1944, tenía 12 parejas de amantes, amigos o parientes pose en su estudio, frente a la cámara en un fondo gris claro, disparado en una cámara blanca de gran formato.

De vuelta a la estación, en la antigua vivienda de los trabajadores ferroviarios, L’Appartement vive hasta su nombre. Richard Billingham marca el 30 aniversario de Ray es una risa, publicado en 1996 por el editor de Zurich Walter Keller (Scalo), un libro Stefano Stoll descubrió en Londres en 1997, en la exposición “Sensation”, donde sus padres lo habían llevado. En la familia, inevitablemente. “De repente entendí que los padres de Richard, Liz y Ray, realmente vivían en dos apartamentos separados”, recuerda. Dos torres de la misma finca del concejo, en Margaret Thatcher’s Inglaterra. Fishtank (1998) juega en una habitación pintada para igualar. “Fuimos como peces en un tanque”, Richard Billingham dijo una vez al director, que saca su propia moral de ella: “Nosotros, en nuestras casas suizas tibias, aprendemos a vivir con muy poco caos. Al final, el caos es la vida”.

En el Château de l’Aile, donde no se permite una sola uña, Vik Muniz vuelve a montar, desde miles de fotografías recogidas en los mercados de pulgas, todo lo que un álbum familiar contiene: los cumpleaños de los niños, la boda de los padres, mamá en la playa, la primera bicicleta. Unas habitaciones más adelante, un cambio de dinastía.

En el Musée de la Confrérie des Vignerons, tutora de un festival celebrado cada 25 años, “una vez una generación”, Rineke Dijkstra, un conjunto de los grandes museos del mundo, acordó ser mostrada “en formato de bolsillo”, como Stefano Stoll lo pone. En “Almerisa”, su serie más larga, una joven bosnia se fotografió en 1994, de cinco años de edad

Sobre todo, los visitantes suben al ático del Musée historique, normalmente cerrado al público, para “Shades of Time 2.0”. “Hace veinticinco años, todos nos cautivaron por esta instalación”, recuerda Stefano Stoll. Annelies Štrba, nacido en 1947 en Zug, pasa por cuatro generaciones de su familia: la casa en Melide en el lago Lugano, niños dormidos enteros, la mente marcada La balada de dependencia sexual, reubicado a las orillas de Ticino: el mismo rollo hipnótico, la misma música que sostienen vidas juntas, y la misma ternura para los días ordinarios. El show de diapositivas nunca antes se ha mostrado en Suiza francófona (el Röstigraben muere duro). “También es maravilloso poder mostrar esto a una generación que está empezando a conectarse con la inteligencia artificial”, añade el director.

Una figura importante de la escena mexicana, que representó a su país en la Bienal de Venecia en 2017, Carlos Amorales “no está realmente en la fotografía”, admite Stefano Stoll, al conocerlo en cada visita a la Ciudad de México. Excepto en 1996. Como estudiante en Amsterdam, inventó Los Amorales, una lucha libre alter ego usando una máscara lanzada desde su propia cara, en una cultura donde la máscara es sagrada: "un luchador nunca quita su máscara, en el dolor de perder toda su carrera", señala el director. Larga renuencia a reabrir ese capítulo, el artista dio en el 30 aniversario de su propia vida oriental, seleccionó 150 diapositivas de cientos y los animaba con inteligencia artificial

Otra liturgia: el fútbol. En el Cinéma Astor, Zidane: Un retrato del siglo XXI El 23 de abril de 2005, Douglas Gordon y Philippe Parreno entrenaron 17 cámaras en el Real Madrid número 5 mientras se enfrentaba a Villarreal, desde el inicio hasta la tarjeta roja final, fijada a una puntuación de Mogwai. “El fútbol es algo que une naciones y familias, y tanto divide naciones y familias”, señala Stefano Stoll, habiendo traído a los medios de fútbol amateur para que los fans deportivos de la misma imagen puedan compartir Sábado noche de fiebre "Todavía sentí que me faltaba algo con un poco de gracia", admite el director de Imágenes Vevey. En Rue d'Italie, Erika Stucky, reina del yodel con jazz, revela 44 años de fotografías proyectadas detrás de ella en conciertos, su familia de sangre y su familia musical pétrenos el fin de semana, empezando por sus primeros padres de baile.

No familia escapa del dolor, dice un proverbio chino Stefano Stoll ha hecho suyo. En el Jardin de l’Oyonne, en Quai Roussy, Deanna Dikeman se despide, durante 27 años consecutivos. En 1991, dejar su casa de padres en Sioux City, Iowa, el fotógrafo americano disparó su ola de su coche. El gesto se convirtió en un ritual.

Otra pena, Castillo. Erik Kessels, que una vez llenó una iglesia Vevey con 350.000 imágenes, regresa con una sola. La de su hermana Susan, golpeada por un coche a las nueve, cuando tenía 11 años: la última fotografía que sus padres podían encontrar de ella, tomada en un parque de diversiones. Una imagen se extiende sin etiquetar a través de las ventanas de Vevey, en carteles, en la marcha de la prensa

En el Musée Jenisch, que reúne a los laureados del Gran Premio, Amandine Marchand, a cargo de Éditions Images Vevey, lleva a los visitantes a una tienda inusual. “Undercover Pleasures” toma su nombre de la tienda de sexo Pacifico Silano los padres corrieron en Nueva Jersey cuando era un tío casi.

Los objetos, también, tienen sus historias familiares. Frente al lago, cerca del Alimentarium, una vez sede de Nestlé, Tokuko Ushioda remata ocho diptychs, el refrigerador cerrado, el refrigerador abierto, fotografiado en hogares de Tokio entre 1981 y 1995. Brillat-Savarin, edición de aperitivos. “Dime cómo guardas tu nevera, dime lo que comes, y te diré lo que es bueno

Por último, la Salle del Castillo. JR, cuyos monumentales proyectos 2010 y 2012 ayudaron a Images Vevey “tomar”, en palabras de Stefano Stoll, marca el 15 aniversario de “Inside Out” aquí. Vevey fue uno de los primeros puestos internacionales del proyecto: 5.200 retratos filmados en tres semanas, en el 2012. Dos cubos se enfrentan uno al otro.

Imágenes Vevey Biennial, “Somos familia!”, 10a edición, 5 a 27 de septiembre, 2026, Vevey (Suiza). Unos cincuenta proyectos, gratuitos; exposiciones cubiertas abren diariamente de 11 a.m. a 7 p.m.

items.title: Las últimas imágenes tomadas dentro del World Trade Center
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Las últimas imágenes tomadas dentro del World Trade Center

En el verano de 2001, un electricista de noche vagaba por los suelos vacíos del World Trade Center con una cámara digital, oficinas de fotografía, cocinas y escaleras que nadie más pensaba grabar. Veinticinco años después, para el aniversario del 11 de septiembre, Blind publica este conjunto de imágenes históricas.

 

Por Jonas Cuénin. Fotos de Konstantin Petrov.

Konstantin Petrov llegó a Nueva York desde Estonia en 1998, trabajando en trabajos eléctricos sin licencia antes de aterrizar un trabajo más estable. En junio de 2001, tomó una posición nocturna en Windows en el mundo, el restaurante ocupando los pisos 106 y 107 de la Torre Norte. De día era el superintendente de un edificio de apartamentos en Manhattan; por la noche, solo en las torres después de que las oficinas se desplomaron, llevó su cámara.

Durante ese verano, filmó involucrados de fotografías digitales: banquetes y escenarios de mesa para el servicio del día siguiente, accesorios de ascensor, esconces, escaleras, equipo de cocina. Desde más de 1.300 pies arriba, su ojo también alcanzó el saltoiendo sobre un inactivo Manhattan, la ciudad visible a través del vidrio que nadie más miraba a esa hora.

Petrov compartió las imágenes en Fotki, un sitio temprano de intercambio de fotos estonio iniciado por su amigo Dmitri Don. “World Trade Center es, como, tan genial,” Don más tarde recordó a los dos de ellos diciendo cuando Petrov consiguió el trabajo, una línea que todavía dio años después, una vez que las torres se habían ido y la observación había tomado un peso diferente.

En la mañana del 11 de septiembre, Petrov terminó su turno y salió del garaje del sótano del edificio. Ya se había ido cuando el primer avión golpeó, y no comprendió lo que había pasado hasta llegar a casa y dio la vuelta a las noticias.

Las fotografías se quedaron sin darse cuenta hasta 2014, cuando el cineasta Erik Nelson, investigó una película National Geographic llamada 9/10: Las horas finales, encontró el archivo Fotki de Petrov y utilizó 44 de las imágenes. Petrov nunca vio ese reconocimiento: murió en un accidente de motocicleta en la West Side Highway de Manhattan en 2002, menos de un año después de los ataques.

Las fotografías de Konstantin Petrov siguen siendo uno de los únicos registros interiores del World Trade Center desde sus últimos meses, habitaciones vacías y vistas tranquilas tomadas por alguien sin razón para pensar que les importaría. Veinticinco años más tarde, se destacan por sí solos: un archivo privado del electricista de turno nocturno, publicado ahora como la última mirada dentro de un edificio que ya no existe.

items.title: Mujeres Fotógrafos Roban el foco
items.content:
Cientos de héroes, dedicados a promover y defender a las mujeres fotógrafas, comienzan con una observación que hace mucho tiempo ha desaparecido: detrás de los mayores retratos de las estrellas del siglo XX, casi siempre había una mujer detrás de la lente. Su ambición es restaurar a estas mujeres al centro de la historia fotográfica — una historia que ayudaron a escribir, de la que han sido borrados con demasiada frecuencia.

Para las primeras obras de la exposición, Cientos Heroines se han asociado con Hermanas de los Lens, una organización dedicada a la promoción de las mujeres fotógrafas que trabajaron entre los años 1850 y 1960, que ha puesto a disposición de esta exposición impresos originales raros.

Tres pioneros injustamente olvidados son llevados a la luz: Lallie Charles, una fotógrafa irlandesa con sede en Londres y uno de los retratistas de la sociedad más célebre de la época eduiana: Dorothy Wilding, la primera mujer nombrada como Fotógrafo Oficial Real de la Corona Británica, cuyos retratos de Elizabeth II aparecieron en sellos de correo británico; y Madame D’Ora, una fotógrafatro austría austría austriaca que se estableció primero en Viena, después en París desde 1925 en París, de moda, de 1925 hacia la sociedad.

Estos pioneros inmortalizaron, entre otros, la actriz británica Vivien Leigh, a quien el mundo se encontró por primera vez en Se fue con el viento (1939), el animador estadounidense Tallulah Bankhead, y la estrella alemana-americana Marlene Dietrich, el icono supremo del cine pre-guerra.

El fotógrafo sudafricano Jillian Edelstein, nacido en Ciudad del Cabo y con sede en Londres desde la década de 1980, domina la sección contemporánea de la exposición. Entrenado en fotoperiodismo y publicado en la New York Times Magazine y Vogue, ella persigue en cada retrato "la humanidad detrás de la máscara de la celebridad, la persona detrás de la persona."

Entre las imágenes más poderosas de Edelstein está su retrato del fallecido diseñador británico Vivienne Westwood, quien murió en 2022, disparado con su pelo salvaje de color llama y dos cuernos de plata pequeños clavados en sus rizos, su expresión apareció en algún lugar entre la maldad y la majestad. Amy Winehouse, el prodigioso talentoso alma británica y cantante de jazz que murió a los 27 en 2011, aparece con brazos plegados y mirada un icono crudo.

El archivo de Elisabeth Buchmeyer-Lewis, un fotógrafo británico especializado en el mundo de la música de finales del siglo XX, proporciona un contrapunto eléctrico. Sus imágenes se sumergen en el mundo backstage del rock y jazz británico de los años 70 y 1980: Ian Dury, cantante, lyricista y fundador de los Blockheads, arropado sobre su micrófono en el legendario 100 Club de Oxford Street, junto con fotografías previamente no visibles

En conjunto, estos retratos miden todo el alcance de lo que las fotógrafas dieron a la cultura pop, y al siglo que la consumió. “Stardust” pone el registro en claro.

“Stardust: 100 Years of Stage, Screen and Celebrity” por cientos de héroes está a la vista de la nueva Hundred Heroines Foto Museum en Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, Reino Unido, del 11 de septiembre al 20 de noviembre de 2026. Entrada gratuita.

items.title: An Instrument Called Photography
items.content:
One photograph can hide another. This is the very essence of Dysnomia Live, a performance born from a foundational body of work developed by Alexandre Dupeyron over several years. Evolving from a slideshow exchanged a decade ago between a photographer and a double bassist—an interaction that was tentative and almost accidental—into its current performance-based format, the duo continually pushes the dialogue between their disciplines further. In 2022, a system inspired by VJing—the practice of manipulating live video imagery borrowed from club culture and concerts—transformed the image into an instrument in its own right. It is a production of Collectif Déluge. A man stands in the dark, a triggering interface beneath his fingers. Images appear, overlap, dissolve to the rhythm of the double bass. Since then, the performance, 70 minutes long, has been staged around twenty times, at Fotografiska in Shanghai, the Blue Note in Beijing, and FRAC Méca in Bordeaux, taking on, depending on the stage, the form of dance, calligraphy, sometimes another language. “On stage, photography leaves behind its stillness to become living matter, which I manipulate in real time like an instrument in dialogue with the musicians,” says Alexandre Dupeyron.

The performance unfolds around three ontological questions: where do we come from, what are we, where are we going? “Silent Green” shifts that arc sideways, leaving behind our hubris to look at the world from within the living rather than above it. This shift draws on two photographic bodies of work. Ashes of the Future traces the paths of fire in Australia, France and the United States, where Dupeyron worked with researchers from the Rocky Mountain Research Station and the US Department of Agriculture’s Fire Lab, who study fire rather than extinguish it. Pinus Pinaster (2023) turns to pioneer plants and their capacity to recolonize damaged soil, to split through asphalt. “From dehumanized megacities to the resurgence of the wild, the performance unfolds a visual and sonic cosmogony,” Dupeyron sums up. Humanity becomes pharmakon here, both poison and cure.

Thomas Julienne reorchestrated the entire score for this new chapter. A string trio, two violins and a cello, joins the original lineup. Four new compositions were written specifically for the occasion, hovering between avant-garde jazz, post-rock and contemporary music. The composer also leads the quintet Theorem of Joy, whose album Feux was named best jazz album of 2025 by the magazine Paris Move, which praised “a radical album, not through provocation, but through grace.”

On the visual side, fifteen years of research and archival sedimentation feed the stagecraft. Alexandre Dupeyron assembles and manipulates his black-and-white photographs live, building an underground visual arc that traces our presence in the world, from its origins to the fractures of contemporary megacities. Photography acts here as an autonomous narrative engine, on equal footing with the music.

For the world premiere, on Sunday at Pioneer Works (Brooklyn), the ensemble welcomes drummer Ches Smith, a longtime collaborator of John Zorn and Marc Ribot. Rounding out the lineup are Ellinoa on vocals, Dylan Ebrahimian on violin, Julie Kim on cello, Dustin Carlson on guitar and Alix Tucou on trombone and keyboard. Each night, the sequence of images reinvents itself; there is no preset score of visuals.

The following day at Picto, the format tightens into a quartet: Dupeyron, Julienne on double bass, Ellinoa and Alix Tucou on bass trombone. Julienne pushes the double bass toward preparations and sonic friction, turning the instrument into a filter for the world’s raw pulse. A session conceived as a more intimate variation on the same dialogue.

The press has followed this journey. In French cultural magazine Télérama, Thierry Voisin writes that Thomas Julienne’s compositions tell “a story of the blue planet, from the formation of the earth to the final explosion.” For Fabien Ribery, in L’Intervalle, the performance sits “somewhere between the dark romanticism of Gérard de Nerval, the science-fiction experiments of Chris Marker and the metaphysical noir of Jean-Luc Godard’s Alphaville.”

In 2023, Dysnomia Live also received the “L’art de la reprise” prize (SACEM, ONDA, Institut Français), and Alexandre Dupeyron and Thomas Julienne are 2025 Villa Albertine laureates. This New York residency comes with cultural mediation workshops for music and art schools, in which the two artists introduce the concept of ecosophy, coined by Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss, for whom man is not at the top of the hierarchy of life but rather part of the ecosphere. A residency project is also under discussion with the Brooklyn Music School and the International Center of Photography, pairing five photographer-musician duos around an original piece. The tour continues in October at the Musée de la mer in Bordeaux.

The book Dysnomia, which gathers this same archival work, serves as the matrix for the performance: each visual chapter finds its answer in a composition by Theorem of Joy. “Through his work, Alexandre Dupeyron has built, across his series, uninterrupted conversations from which emerges the sense of a universal matter, like a black hole,” writes exhibition curator François Cheval in the book’s afterword. “A luminous energy bursts forth, like a vital source, asserting the presence of being as essence.”

Acoustic session, Monday, September 14, 2026, 7:30 PM, Picto NY, 77 Washington Avenue, Brooklyn (limited capacity, RSVP required).

items.title: Irina Rozovsky’s Balkan Wandering
items.content:
Mountain Black Heart opens on a dedication to “the miracle.” Three images follow, by way of prologue: a bedroom window opens onto a ceiling light that, at first glance, might be mistaken for a full moon. The next image catches a child mid-cartwheel in the tall grass at dusk. Then comes an apparition worthy of a fairy tale: the immaculate train of a bird, possibly a white peacock, perched at night in a tree. Irina Rozovsky sets out her terms here: joy and wonder sit alongside a muted unease, one that the darkness of night only sharpens.

But the miracle is slow to arrive: the book’s opening pages plunge us into cold. Nocturnal images follow one another, ruins mingling with barbed wire, plasterboard, planks of wood. A black cat slips past. A woman with a bandaged eye and a figure stretched out on a bare bench are photographed on public transport, bundled into their coats. Snow leaves its trace on a fur coat. Fog engulfs a dirt path lined with wire fencing, the whole scene faintly uncanny.


Nor can we tell whether it is dawn or nightfall, and the artist will not enlighten us. No image is captioned, no country named. Born in Moscow in 1981 and brought to the United States as a child in the wake of the Soviet Jewish exodus of the 1980s, Irina Rozovsky carries a diffuse cultural familiarity with the Slavic world, one born of a history she did not live through herself yet that runs through her all the same. When she is not on the road, she lives and works in Athens, Georgia, where she co-directs the photography space The Humid with her husband, the photographer Mark Steinmetz.

Her wanderings here are not, then, a return to any point of origin: the sense of remembrance these images stir has no precise object. No narrative thread holds them together. The work proceeds in fragments. Since 2014, Irina Rozovsky has kept returning to these territories — Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, Croatia, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania — in what she calls “a type of travel diary or personal journalism,” moving by rental car, bus, and train, crossing the borders of nations recently formed and re-formed.

This method has already proven itself: In One to Nothing (2009), Island in My Mind (2015), and then In Plain Air (2021) already bore its mark. This time, the artist attempts to “sketch a geography of heart and mind,” at the cost, at times, of a disquiet she does not shy away from. As with the image of a newborn laid straight on the ground, swaddled in a white onesie, surrounded by plastic bags and threadbare blankets at the foot of a tree, in the dark. Is it absolute precarity, or an ordinary campsite? Impossible to say. Irina Rozovsky’s photography is enigmatic: she withholds the key, leaving the viewer’s eye to construct, alone, whatever it believes it sees.

Menace coils itself into small details. From the book’s earliest pages, a large dog appears behind iron bars, jaws open. Further on, laminated banners hung from a tree bear the portraits of men, likely the victims of a massacre whose location and circumstances remain unnamed. A car crash follows, then the fleeting sight of a cemetery. Though the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s are never shown head-on, a tension bears down on each of these images, like a buried memory.

Elsewhere, a blonde woman at her window raises her arm in a gesture resembling a Nazi salute. Irina Rozovsky offers no comment. She saw. She kept the image. When she photographs a blond boy set down in the night grass, an albino python coiled around him, the harsh flash brings out the whiteness of the snake and of the child alike against the pitch dark. Natural empathy contends with a discomfort, muted and indefinable. It is this quality of unease that Irina Rozovsky cultivates, fascinated, she says, by “the struggle and endurance that pulses through a place damaged by history.”

From the very darkest of these pages, light also rises. A woman strokes the scruff of a brindle mastiff, an abandoned Soviet-era car rusting on the hillside behind them. An elderly woman smiles tenderly as she feeds pigeons. A child stands on his hands in a field of wildflowers. A loose puppy plays with a watermelon. A horse grazes on grass dotted with poppies before the expanse of a lake. Water asserts itself, gradually, as a recurring, calming presence. Like breath itself.

From beneath a glass table, on which rest an Ottoman lamp, a jug, and a coloured glass, the artist frames a blonde woman, an apparition against a blue sky. This inverted vantage point, where everything seems weightless, conveys less a place or a face than a state of grace. It seems to answer the “humanity” the artist says she has found here, and “the bright gravity” of the people she meets.

In the book’s final images, at the edge of a lake, a scarlet streak and a scattering of empty Coca-Cola bottles stain the crystalline water and its shore. Dye, or blood? The question is left hanging, much like the past itself, forever poised to resurface.

Mountain Black Heart (2026) by Irina Rozovsky is published by Mack and available for $75.
items.excerpt: The American photographer of Russian origin lets herself drift through the countries of former Yugoslavia and their neighbours. Published by Mack, Mountain Black Heart oscillates between unease and wonder, borne along by an unsettled familiarity with these territories.

items.title: Camille Vivier Sculpts the Flesh
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Camille Vivier Sculpts the Flesh

Only a few days remain to discover the first major retrospective the Maison Européenne de la Photographie devotes to Camille Vivier in Paris. A mesmerising journey in which bodybuilders, puppets and votive candles vie for the title of most beautiful living sculpture.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Camille Vivier.

For over twenty-five years, Camille Vivier’s eye has moved with rare fluency between fashion commissions and fine-art photography, two facets of a single obsession: probing what, within a body, already borders on statuary. Beginning her career in the late 1990s, she has forged a body of work in which glamour never stops flirting with the uncanny, where classical beauty is always shadowed by a whiff of unease.

At the heart of this retrospective reigns the female nude, unfurled through figures who have shaken the very foundations of conventional femininity. Sophie, Tjiki, Deborah: three bodybuilders with spectacular musculature, captured in stagings where the body reveals itself as raw material to be sculpted, a living architecture that rivals marble torsos.

One cannot help but think of the portraits Robert Mapplethorpe made of Lisa Lyon, who became the first world champion of women’s bodybuilding in 1979 and went on to be the American photographer’s muse in the 1980s, a direct wellspring for the “Sophie” series, born of the same fascination with anatomies that confound the assignment of gender.

The exhibition also unleashes an entire bestiary of anthropomorphic objects, summoned as much for their symbolic weight as their sheer visual strangeness: ritual candles drawn from Afro-Brazilian traditions, avant-garde puppets by Luigi Veronesi, a leading figure of 1930s Italian abstraction, biomechanical sets inherited from the world of H.R. Giger, the Swiss artist behind the creature in Alien.

This sweeping journey through nearly a hundred works, gelatin silver and digital prints, Polaroids, pieces conceived especially for the occasion, paints the portrait of an artist for whom photography remains, above all, a tool of illusion and metamorphosis, where the animate and the inanimate carry on a thoroughly illicit correspondence.

 

 

 

The exhibition “Camille Vivier” runs at the MEP in Paris, France, until September 13, 2026.

items.title: “Let’s Celebrate!”: Everyone’s Own Party, a Party for All
items.content:
Two faces all but disappear behind a flurry of multicoloured fans, caught mid-motion in a gesture that owes as much to dance as to parade. The scene could pass for a Magnum dispatch, so squarely does it favour a perfect composition. It was, in fact, taken in 2019, by a photographer nobody, a year earlier, had ever heard of. That is the whole premise of “Let’s Celebrate!”: blur the generations and keep only the moment.

Confetti

YellowKorner turned twenty, and has spent those twenty years defending one conviction: photography deserves to be shared, for everyone’s pleasure, and has no business staying locked inside contemporary art fairs. Twenty years spent opening galleries everywhere, from Bordeaux to Shanghai (eighty of them today), offering fine-art prints to private buyers and collectors alike. To mark the occasion, the house set photographers a simple brief: send us your celebration, the real one, yours, with your partner, your friends, your family, the one from your hometown, from your happiest moments.

What strikes you first is that no two images look alike. Some chose celebration in its most literal sense: crowds, confetti, paper streamers. Others preferred to render it obliquely: a solitary body, a beam of light, a held breath. The selection embraces that range, as if the word “celebration” only made sense in the plural. There is pure documentary alongside near-choreographed gesture, street and studio, saturated colour and austere black and white. The thread, thin but real, is a shared urgency: each photographer seems to have wanted to capture something that, a second later, would already be gone.

The geography, meanwhile, reads like a trip around the world in twenty frames. Alexandra Buxbaum checks in from Arizona, Olesia Kim from Tyumen, Eleonora Laufer from Buenos Aires, Yevhen Samuchenko from Odessa. In Brighton, Liban Elmi captured three boys wading into the sea arm in arm, backs to the camera, caught in the same motion. “Laughter crosses borders more easily than words,” the photographer wrote in his application, a line that alone sums up the spirit of the series. In Nandgaon, Vivek Goyal plunged into clouds of coloured powder during the Holi festival, where men and women douse each other until the pigment erases every face. “Colour becomes the ageless language of human connection,” he wrote. In Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer, Roxane Mo captured another register of celebration, closer to carnival than ritual: in “Flamboyer” (“Blaze”), a woman in a sequinned dress screams with joy under an orange hoop, surrounded by a costumed parade at the Pete the Monkey eco-festival. The image, an emblem of the series, sums up on its own what the whole selection is after: collective joy, unfiltered, full of colour and expression.

Memory

Head down a floor into the YellowKorner space, and an entirely different season opens up, more intimate: the season of memory sold at the counter. “Colorful,” the cult collection that built YellowKorner’s finest hours, has been reissued and expanded for a confidential, exclusive edition: twenty images to choose from, each delivered in its own dedicated case. Laurent Baheux returns with his African animals, in black and white, without an ounce of sentimentality. Matthieu Ricard suspends a Tibetan monk in meditation, outside of time, precisely what the La Hune gallery upstairs is celebrating. Thibaud Poirier files away his Trinity College library, a paper temple that could almost pass for a nave. Also featured: Formento+Formento, Pedro Jarque Krebs, Tull & Bruno Morandi, Nicolas Velter, Jakub Polomski, Bernhard Hartmann, Ruslan Bolgov, Ludwig Favre, Nicolas Bets, LDK, Fabien Novarino, Alexandre Fauve, Damien Dufresne, Robbie McIntosh, Mina Mimbu, Andrea Pavan. A roster of names whose prints are often sold out, now available again, ready to hang on your own wall.

Round Dance

Back in the exhibition, what still stands out is the absence of hierarchy between names you know and names you’re discovering. YellowKorner has always defended the idea that photography deserves to be accessible to everyone. The hang makes that case almost literally: no caption reveals who already had a career and who is just starting one. Laurent Paillier, who photographs dancers carved out by coloured light in an echo of Lucio Fontana slashing his canvases, may put it best: “It celebrates the living body, dance as a form of absolute happiness, light as a metaphor for life, and gesture as an act of freedom.” It should be added that this celebration reads less like a retrospective than a prologue. YellowKorner is changing face, reinventing its artistic direction, opening its doors wider to women photographers, to documentary approaches, to aesthetics owing less and less to the male gaze that long dominated the genre. Twenty years on, and the next chapter is already being written, somewhere between a case being closed and a fan unfolding.

“Let’s Celebrate!”, exhibition at La Hune gallery, Paris, September 19 to October 10, 2026. Opening night September 24, 2026. “Colorful” collection, on view in the YellowKorner-La Hune space on the ground floor, September 16 to October 14, 2026. All “Let’s Celebrate!” photographs are available for purchase on the YellowKorner website.

items.title: Visa pour l’Image: The World we “Must Keep Looking at”
items.content:
Thank you. Stephan Vanfleteren’s 2018 portrait of Jean-François Leroy is everywhere in Perpignan. Thirty-eight years ago, he co-founded what has become an unmissable gathering for the photojournalism family. He died on August 31, two days after the opening of this year’s edition of Visa pour l’image, “his baby.” He was 69.

That same evening, at the festival’s ritual opening screening at the Campo Santo, the 2,500 spectators in attendance rose to their feet. Long applause followed. French President Emmanuel Macron paid tribute in a statement to “the memory of a passionate journalist,” “a tireless defender of photojournalism.”

“A tribute he would have said he didn’t care about, but that he would have bragged about every two minutes,” smiled Delphine Lelu, his longtime associate, visibly moved. She and the rest of the festival’s team are picking up where he left off. “We will keep Visa alive in keeping with the values Jean-François defended.”

“A visual culture melting pot”

This year again, Visa pour l’image proved itself the crossroads of the profession: the place where people gather over a drink at the Café de la Poste, between two exhibitions at the Église des Dominicains, in the warmth of the halls at the Couvent des Minimes, or at the evening screenings to see colleagues’ work. Visa is a place of fellowship among people of the image.

In his legacy book, Le Devoir de regarder (The Duty to Look), Jean-François Leroy said as much: “This visual culture melting pot means that, every year, photographers, who are solitary the rest of the year, meet, look at each other, and exchange, from the most established to the beginners.”

Thus Raymond Depardon, a towering figure who had never before exhibited on Perpignan’s walls, appeared alongside a younger generation: Jerôme Gence, Robin Tutenges, Elise Blanchard, and Philémon Barbier. A happy mix, mutual admiration between two eras, a passing of the torch between generations. “Visa pour l’image’s mantra, for thirty-eight years, has remained the same: discovering young photographers, confirming and highlighting the work of established ones, and rediscovering ‘historic’ photographers of the past,” Jean-François Leroy wrote in his book.

In a profession whose economy is more precarious than ever, Visa is a lighthouse in the dark, a vital source of support. “What matters most to us is distributing 21 awards worth more than 160,000 euros. That’s serious help toward production,” Delphine Lelu points out.

Holding onto the truth

For nearly forty years, more than 220,000 visitors have come to look the world in the face (see this year’s full program here), taking the time to move from photo to photo, reading every introductory text, every caption. “Jean-François Leroy stood for holding onto the truth. That was all that mattered to him. He cared about showing the world as it is, without filters, while also making sure the information could reach as wide a public as possible,” Delphine Lelu recalls.

Coming to Visa means facing the gaze of young Afghan girls sold into marriage to support their families (Elise Blanchard), of virtual unions in Japan with manga characters (Jérôme Gence), diving into the depths of the oceans (Laurent Ballesta) as much as into the bowels of Chernobyl (Gerd Ludwig). It means confronting the news head-on: the agony of civilians in Gaza, the terror of drones in Ukraine, the forgotten wars of Ethiopia, Cambodia, or Sudan. It means putting a face to numbers: 1.5 million people affected by illiteracy in France (Jérémy Lempin), illustrating a geography, that of cocaine (Mads Nissen) or the exile of young Guinean minors (Hervé Lequeux).

Coming to Visa pour l’image means seeing the world at its worst, but also at its best. A world we “must keep looking at, even when looking at it is uncomfortable,” as Jean-François Leroy put it.

“AI has made authentic images suspect”

Visa has often been shunned by institutional circles. Ministerial visits are rare, and subsidies are meager compared with those given to the Rencontres d’Arles. “Visa pour l’image, that’s just boom-boom stuff,” one advisor at the Ministry of Culture once said. No comment.

As photography marks its bicentennial, the Perpignan festival reminds us every year that photojournalism cannot be treated as a lesser genre of the medium. Quite the opposite: this has been Visa’s fight since its first edition, in 1989. Jean-François Leroy put it in his own way: “As if photographing a war, a family, or a revolution were somehow less noble than photographing a lemon on a table.”

Visa serves the public good. The festival’s mission to educate people on how to look and how to understand information has never been more essential than today. In the age of artificial intelligence, generated images, and deepfakes, learning to look has become a societal priority. “AI has made authentic images suspect by contamination,” Jean-François Leroy warned.

The festival’s week dedicated to schoolchildren is precious. It should be extended to every school, given how vital the stakes are. Forewarned is forearmed. “I maintain that Visa pour l’image’s greatest value today is this education of the eye that we strive to uphold. Younger generations need to learn how to look, because soon, as adults and citizens, it will be their duty to do so,” Jean-François Leroy wrote.

An education through images that mattered so much to him, as did his support for the new generation of photographers. “Your camera doesn’t make you a photojournalist. Your ability to build a story with a series of images that have a beginning, a middle, and an end, that’s what makes you a photojournalist,” he wrote in a letter that now reads as a kind of testament. To pass it on so that photojournalism and its values endure, so that Visa pour l’image continues to bear witness to the world, so that we can keep looking at it as it truly is.

38th International Photojournalism Festival of Perpignan, Visa pour l’image, until September 13, 2026.

*« Le Devoir de regarder. Histoires et réflexions sur le photojournalisme » (The Duty to Look: Stories and Reflections on Photojournalism), Jean-François Leroy in conversation with Isabelle Fougère, is is published by Éditions Mkf and available for €20.
items.excerpt: The 38th edition of the international photojournalism festival in Perpignan was marked by mourning, following the death of its co-founder, Jean-François Leroy. An essential rendezvous for the profession, Visa pour l’image continues to teach us to look the world in the face.

items.title: William Meyers: Beyond the Bully Pulpit
items.content:
In a Brooklyn subway station, William Meyers captured in 2015 a scene of deceptive ordinariness. Beside an elderly man lying on the platform, victim of an epileptic seizure, a woman kneels over him, watching. Her expression holds both urgency and solicitude. How many such gestures go unseen every day, for lack of a witness?

Film and full frame, negative border included: William Meyers’s method is inflexible. He forbids himself any cropping, entrusting his negatives to Chuck Kelton, a master printer whose New York laboratory is one of the last true sanctuaries of traditional silver printing. The monochrome asserts itself. “Black and white, because it’s a somewhat archaic technology, contributes significance,” he says, “like playing Bach on period musical instruments.”

A successive naval air intelligence officer in the United States Navy Reserve, staffer on a Senate subcommittee on poverty and employment, businessman and photography critic for the Wall Street Journal, William Meyers came to photographic practice in his fifties. This passage through American public life permeates every frame.

The photography critic Vicki Goldberg, whom he readily quotes, wrote: “Vision probably draws as much from the life as from the eye, from the heart as well as the brain, from the complexities of personality more than from ingenuity or mastery of craft.” Only a man who has served, deliberated, and moved through the back rooms of public life could photograph democracy with this particular intimacy, neither naive nor cynical.

From this emerges a radical formal decision: to stand in the ranks rather than face the podium. In the essay accompanying the work, journalist Nicole Gelinas notes that the images that persist in her memory are peopled with “backs of heads and shoulders.” William Meyers explains: “By having someone between the camera and the action, I put the viewer of the picture in the audience, recreating the experience of being there, not just showing what it looks like.”


At the City Council hearing in August 2017, a massive silhouette interposes itself in the foreground, while the room opens behind it onto portraits of George Washington and the Marquis de Lafayette, television cameramen, journalists, and rows of citizens come to testify. It is not power that William Meyers seeks to document here, but the vigilance of those who watch over it.

This perspective produces some of his most striking images. On Broadway, a homeless man sleeps on the pavement in front of the closed window of a Victoria’s Secret lingerie store: the face of a mannequin, behind the lowered blinds, looms over the scene. On Madison Avenue in the snow, an inflatable union rat, symbol of American labor protest, doubles itself in the reflection of a glass facade, its claws seemingly threatening a passerby.

“An important aspect of any art is the significant juxtaposition of key elements,” notes William Meyers. “I work at it.” While he claims the influence of Henri Cartier-Bresson, sharing his full-frame discipline, he puts it in service of a civic grammar rather than a mere poetics of the moment.

Civil Society at Work

Civics is organized around seven thematic chapters, two of which did not exist when the project was first shown at the Nailya Alexander Gallery in New York in 2016: “Social Capital” and “Civic Markers.” “I came to believe that democracy was as much a cultural phenomenon as a political one,” the photographer confides, “the markers, both formal and casual, remind us of what we have to be grateful for.”

In “Social Capital,” five of the thirteen images are shot in a place of worship, a synagogue or a church, during a blood drive or a CPR training session. Homeless men are also sheltered on cots. None of these scenes take place in a government office. When the State falls short, citizens step in.

Further on, in the newsroom of the New York Daily News, photographed in March 2015, journalists work at their screens while historic front pages line the walls: “Ford to City: Drop Dead,” “Men Walk on the Moon,” “Who’s a Bum!” Past and present of the news superimpose themselves within a single frame, a reminder that journalism too is a pillar of civic life, fragile, threatened, irreplaceable.


Two images, taken seventeen years apart, trace the book’s horizon. The first, shot in January 2026 on the steps of the Moynihan Courthouse in Manhattan, shows a woman draped in an American flag: she has just been naturalized as an American citizen and looks, says William Meyers, toward “new tomorrows.” The second, taken in May 2009 in Riverside Park, shows Memorial Day wreaths battered by a nocturnal storm.

“The wind-blown memorial wreaths suggest the fragility of their sacrifice,” the photographer adds, “how tenuous their victories and how needful for the living to be mindful.” The future and memory, side by side, without hierarchy. “I have my own political preferences and prejudices,” concedes William Meyers, “but my aim in Civics was not to argue for any particular viewpoints but to concentrate on processes.”

With the same attention and the same distance, he has photographed members of the Westboro Baptist Church, an American sect notoriously known for its hate-filled demonstrations, and a rally in favor of the Ground Zero mosque; the anti-capitalist Occupy Wall Street movement in Zuccotti Park and a march by the deeply conservative Tea Party; a Black Lives Matter banner on Broadway and an assembly standing at an official NYPD promotion ceremony.

Of the Westboro church members, whom he says he detests without reservation, he retains one precise image: “The critical component of the picture is the cop in the foreground who is protecting their right to be despicable. That, and the pedestrians who are exercising their right to ignore them.” Democracy, in this light, is not agreement on values. It is the procedure that allows incompatible convictions to coexist without destroying each other.

Civics by William Meyers is published by Apollo Publishers and available for $50.
items.excerpt: With Civics, the New York photographer draws a portrait of ordinary democracy. An inhabited, grave, and luminous work, arriving as the United States marks its 250th anniversary.

items.title: Photography Takes the Pulse of France
items.content:
A white and pink caravan, parked beneath the colonnades of the Palais-Royal. A little further on, beneath the Arc de Triomphe, the same silhouette, towed by a silent gray SUV. Between the two, a mobile analog photography studio, a traveling darkroom, and this line painted on the side: “Step into the darkroom and reveal the portrait of your heart.” It could pass for a contemporary art installation that wandered off course. It is in fact a touring device, designed to crisscross France for over a year. And yes, visitors leave with an image of their own heart.

The LUX Tour officially launched on September 3, 2026, in the courtyard of the Ministry of Culture, at the Jardin du Palais-Royal in Paris. Behind the name stands the LUX Network, which brings together 33 photography festivals and fairs across the country, from Rennes to Bordeaux, from Nîmes to Boulogne-Billancourt. At the heart of the project (the phrase, here, is more than a figure of speech) sits “À l’origine du cœur,” an artistic experience devised by the Trigone collective.

The principle is almost childlike in its simplicity: visitors have electrodes placed on them, their pulse is captured, converted into an electrical impulse, and that impulse exposes a sheet of light-sensitive paper. The deep red of the darkroom. A graduated cylinder, amber developer poured under the glow of a safelight. Then, on the paper, a white branching form spreads like a bolt of lightning, resembling an upside-down tree, or the vessels of a heart traced by electricity itself. Each print is unique, naturally, like every heartbeat.

BMW France, official partner of the venture, does more than put its logo on the trailer. The brand has provided the Trigone collective with the new BMW iX3, fully electric, tasked with towing the caravan and, thanks to its bidirectional Vehicle-to-Load charging technology, powering some of the mobile studio’s equipment. Electricity, in effect, runs through every layer of the project.

There is, in this story, a coincidence BMW is happy to point out. Nicéphore Niépce, the inventor of photography, was also, together with his brother Claude, behind one of the earliest internal combustion engines. Two centuries later, image and mobility find themselves on the same trailer. “This unexpected link between image and mobility resonates strongly with our commitment to the LUX Network,” says Vincent Salimon, chairman of the board of BMW Group France, adding: “We are proud to support a project that brings together heritage, innovation, contemporary creation and the regions.”

The project itself did not begin yesterday. It started at ETPA, the Toulouse photography school, where Paul Baudon built a device capable of amplifying the heart’s electrical signal to trigger an arc that spreads across analog paper. The Trigone collective, which he formed with Anthony Jean and Marianne Thazet, took up the idea in 2021 and has since toured towns, villages and festivals aboard an earlier mobile lab, well before the BMW chapter. Their acknowledged references bring together two figures: the astronomer and illustrator Étienne-Léopold Trouvelot, a pioneer in depicting electrical phenomena in the 19th century, and Hiroshi Sugimoto, whose Lightning Fields series likewise captures electricity directly on film. “A heartbeat is caused by an electrical impulse,” sums up Paul Baudon, adding that the aim is to “materialize the invisible,” the rhythm of life in its most organic form.

From Rennes to Deauville, from Clermont-Ferrand to Céret, the caravan is set to stop at major dates on the French photography calendar, Paris Photo, La Gacilly, the off-circuit of the Rencontres d’Arles, the Mulhouse Biennale, before returning to Paris for Photoclimat in September 2027, exactly a year after its launch. The LUX Tour is in fact just one of three strands of the 200LUX program, labeled part of the Bicentennial of Photography by the Ministry of Culture: alongside it, a Dictionnaire (presque) complet de la photographie (Almost Complete Dictionary of Photography), an editorial project tracing two centuries of history through the eyes of the network’s members, and a group exhibition of all 33 festivals at the MAC, Maison des Arts de Créteil.

Looking at the Trigone collective’s images, one thinks of old X-rays, of laboratory lightning, of the electrical branchings once known as Lichtenberg figures. Inside the caravan, the experience is intense. Once the session ends, the print follows the classic analog path: development, scanning and printing, before being handed to the visitor as a trace of their passage. Everything relies on chemistry and on the operator’s hand, which, for a device designed to run for 13 months across 33 stops, amounts to as much a logistical feat as an artistic one.

More information on the LUX Tour, including full dates and stops, is available here.

items.title: Reap the Earth, Feed Kyoto
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Reap the Earth, Feed Kyoto

Kyoto Farm to Table traces the living roots of Japan’s former capital, where the farmer’s gesture meets the plate with an almost sacred rigor.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Viola Gaskell.

This book springs from the meeting of two complementary voices. Viola Gaskell, an American journalist and photographer from Hawaii, and Momoko Nakamura, a Japanese food writer, joined forces to interview more than thirty producers, chefs, fishermen, and tofu makers across Kyoto.

The city sits atop a singular vegetable heritage, the kyō-yasai, grown for over a thousand years in rich soil fed by exceptionally pure water. The round, plump kamonasu eggplant, the slender kujō-negi leek, and the mild shōgoin-daikon radish rank among the varieties most coveted by high-end kitchens.

This land nurtures shizen shoku, farming free of synthetic inputs, where soil regenerates through compost and crop rotation rather than chemical fertilizer. That philosophy feeds in turn into washoku, the Japanese culinary tradition inscribed by UNESCO on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2013.

Each figure met in this book found their own path toward that philosophy. For some, time abroad was the spark; for others, the Fukushima disaster struck like a warning bell, a call to reconsider the bond between land and body.

Gaskell’s eye had already been sharpened elsewhere, on organic farming in China and on Hong Kong’s vanishing cha chaan tengs, Cantonese diners where Western influence meets local flavor. Kyoto offers her a new terrain of rare intimacy.

 

Kyoto Farm to Table, by Viola Gaskell and Momoko Nakamura, is published by Trope and is available for pre-order at $50.

items.title: Vladimir Seleznev : Quiet, We Pray
items.content:
Start with a sentence, a sign Vladimir Seleznev saw a hundred times before he understood it. In a Russian church, worshippers aren’t gently asked to stay quiet during the service. They’re warned. “Those who talk in the temple are consigned to sorrow and woe,” the sign reads. “If you walk into a church in France and someone asks you not to talk during the service, I think in France it would say please don’t talk. In Russia, it’s written like this,” the artist recalls. The phrase is an instruction manual, and the photographer decided to follow it to the letter, turning it into the title of a project carried out between 2018 and 2024.

This isn’t Seleznev’s first attempt at the subject. Ten years ago, his first book already told the story of an imagined city, a future built on the model of Soviet utopias and then abandoned, a ghost city conceived in echo of Le Corbusier wanting to raze the center of Paris. The book was published by Meduza, an opposition outlet now banned in Russia. At the time, a handful of strangers bought it from France. “It was my first book, and in my opinion, it was excellent,” he says, not bothering with false modesty. It’s out of that decade-long project that the next, harsher idea was born: understanding the instruments by which power shapes a people. “What interests me are the instruments the government, the politicians, use to influence people,” he explains. Religion, historical memory, collective representations: the list is short, but it’s enough.

The starting point is an observation owed to Alexei Tolstoy. The writer, in a novel devoted to Ivan the Terrible, noted that what was most striking wasn’t that such a tyrant had existed, but that there could have existed “a society that watched him without indignation.” Seleznev grew up in that very society, in a devout family. “I’m completely materialist myself, but it’s very hard to rid yourself of that system,” he says. The system in question has its statistics: three churches opened every day in Russia, the word God written into the Constitution since 2020, a Criminal Code article that has punished offending believers’ feelings since 2013. It also has its promised martyrs. The Patriarch calls the coronavirus epidemic divine mercy, the president assures that in the event of nuclear war, Russians will go to paradise as martyrs, and in June 2023 the Orthodox Church declared that pacifism is incompatible with its teaching. There is no authority except from God, says the Epistle to the Romans. In Russia, the line has had quite a career.

How do you photograph an ideology that won’t be photographed? Seleznev documents almost nothing. He composes. A wax hand sold as a relic, bought exactly as found. An in-utero baptism, a medieval rite he saw resurface on Russian social media and staged just as described, “because it still exists, it really exists.” A naked man kneeling in the icy January water, a ritual gesture he describes without apology: “Religious people in Russia have this strict idea of always plunging into cold water, maybe you can get sick, it doesn’t matter, they do it anyway.” And those objects of molten wax, halfway between icon and wound, which he shapes himself in his studio by melting and then burning cones, before lighting them with a single flash carried from scene to scene. “Gregory Crewdson has many light sources, I only have one, but I get a great result,” he says.

These distorted icons, torsos split open, faces erased, bear a family resemblance to Lucio Fontana’s slashed canvases, whose religious ceramics the artist discovered only afterward, as a spectator of his own work. “I hadn’t seen that when I was making my photos, but now I can see the connection,” he admits. One also thinks, watching a nighttime procession by a lake where the faithful advance on their knees, candles in hand, of Werner Herzog’s documentary Bells from the Deep, and of the legend of Kitezh, the holy city popular belief says lies sunken, which the faithful expect to see rise again every year. Seleznev doesn’t cite Herzog out of authorial flourish: he re-enacts the gesture, the kneeling, the walk around the lake, before recognizing the connection himself.

He carries the paradox without grandstanding. To dismantle a language, you have to speak it. “I use the visual language of religious painting against religion,” he sums up, before citing a Russian proverb about fighting an enemy with his own weapon. The proverb comes at a cost. Seleznev left Russia in 2022, “not because of the project, because of the war,” he says, though the two soon became inseparable. The Russian curators once interested in his work backed away one by one. “Today it’s even forbidden to exhibit a photo with a church in it if there’s anything not quite ideal standing next to it,” he says. The project has been shown only once, in Portugal, at a photography festival. In France, it produces an effect he hadn’t anticipated: “These photos raise the most questions, I was very surprised,” he says, almost amused that it took crossing Europe for his work to finally start speaking.

His mother, he says, remains a fanatical supporter of Vladimir Putin and the war. His daughter, from a first marriage, much less so. Between the two lies an entire country where, he believes, the image of the president and the image of God have ended up merging, for lack of icons to tell them apart. Seleznev, for his part, chose his side long ago: that of the materialist who cannot stop photographing the very thing he cannot shake off.

Vladimir Seleznev, “Those Who Talk in the Temple Are Consigned to Sorrow and Woe,” digital photography, series of 52 photographs, 2018-2024. More information about the artist on his website.

items.title: John Baldessari: Language and Image
items.content:
IN IMAGES

John Baldessari: Language and Image

Pérez Art Museum Miami presents “John Baldessari: The End of the Line”, an exhibition tracing the conceptual artist’s rethinking of photography, video, painting, and the relationship between images, words, and meaning.

By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by John Baldessari.

Language was at the center of John Baldessari’s practice, whether expressed through words, photographs, or film stills. In 1970, he burned most of the paintings he had made between 1953 and 1966, turning the act of destruction into the Cremation Project. The gesture shifted attention away from authorship and the artwork as object, toward the act and thought process of making art. Photography and video documented the moment, while in the following decades Baldessari increasingly worked with found photographs, film stills, and images drawn from an ever-expanding archive of popular culture.

Baldessari obscured faces and other details with colored circles, disrupting the original narratives of mass-media images and creating gaps in meaning. His deceptively economical visual language invited viewers to construct their own connections. “I go back and forth between wanting to be abundantly simple and maddeningly complex,” he once said. The tension captures much of what makes his work so compelling: images that appear immediate, yet become increasingly complex the longer the viewer looks and reflects on them.

The exhibition “John Baldessari: The End of the Line” is on view at the Pérez Art Museum Miami until May 9, 2027.

items.title: Madonna Before Madonna
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Madonna Before Madonna

This is a Madonna in her early twenties, still unknown to the public, that Musichead Gallery, on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, invites us to discover: seven photographers captured her between 1980 and 1985, back when she was still nobody — and already punk to the core.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Marc Canter, Richard Corman, Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Mick Rock, and Mark Weiss.

A girl from Michigan lands alone in New York, ready to do whatever it takes to make it on her own terms: drummer, dancer, author of her own songs. Refusing to let the industry claim her, she turns down a ready-made pop career offered in Paris — where others would have written her songs for her — and heads back to New York to co-write them herself. This is the face of that Madonna, punk, sensual, already at war with the establishment, that “The Rise of the Material Girl” reveals.

In the photographs, her style already reads like a manifesto: a red beret tilted just so, a studded belt, leather cuffs and bracelets stacked to the wrist, torn jeans, a look that’s half dare, half play, a lollipop between her lips like a quiet provocation. Worn denim and crimson lipstick, jewelry piled on in layers: the visual vocabulary of an icon, feminine and defiant in the same breath.

Behind the lens: Richard Corman, who met her by chance in 1983 and photographed her in her Lower East Side apartment; Deborah Feingold, who shot the now-iconic “lollipop series” in 1982, in all of twenty minutes; Gary Heery, the Australian photographer working out of Soho, behind some of her earliest publicity photos; and Mark Weiss, who caught her on the set of MTV in 1984. That same year, the album Like a Virgin would catapult Madonna from anonymity to worldwide fame: the legend of the Madonna with Marilyn’s afterglow was underway.

 

“Madonna: The Rise of the Material Girl (1980–1985)” is on view at Musichead Gallery in Los Angeles, through September 26, 2026.
items.excerpt: This is a Madonna in her early twenties, still unknown to the public, that Musichead Gallery, on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, invites us to discover: seven photographers captured her between 1980 and 1985, back when she was still nobody — and already punk to the core.

items.title: Meeting the Revolution, One Face at a Time
items.content:
For Amin Yousefi, the project began with a photograph that shouldn’t have mattered. Working through an archive in Tehran during the pandemic, he paused over an image of a student gathering from the years of the Iranian Revolution – not a defining historical moment, but an ordinary crowd. Among its faces, one person looked directly into the camera, carrying the unsettling sensation of being addressed by someone he could never have met. One photograph wasn’t enough to trust that feeling. It was only after encountering it again and again across the revolution’s vast photographic archive that the project began to take shape.

Born in Abadan in 1996, Yousefi was thirteen during the disputed 2009 presidential election and the protests that became known as the Green Movement – old enough to witness one rupture in Iran’s history, but to inherit the revolution itself only through photographs, documentaries and annual commemorations. Rather than retelling its history, he followed that intuition, rephotographing archival images through a magnifying loupe until the encounters themselves became the work. “For me,” he says, “it was more about this encounter.”

Photographs made to record a revolution begin, almost against their own nature, to behave like portraits. What emerges is the quiet reciprocity of photography: anonymous crowds give way to individuals who actively acknowledge the photographer’s presence. For a moment, the revolution recedes behind something quieter: the brief acknowledgement between photographer and subject, before history carries them both away. One enlarged face eventually led Yousefi to its owner: pioneering Iranian photojournalist Hengameh Golestan, captured looking towards American photographer David Burnett as he photographed the revolution. Golestan barely remembered the moment, recalling only that Burnett had been, in her words, “a handsome man.” The anecdote gently unsettles any certainty about who is looking at whom, reminding us that photographs rarely belong to a single perspective.

That ambiguity runs throughout the book. Yousefi resists romanticising the crowds’ desire to be photographed, instead contrasting it with the radically different relationship to visibility today, when surveillance has transformed public space. Here, the people gathered wanted to be seen; contemporary protesters, he observes, often seek the opposite. The book’s design quietly reinforces that tension. Each enlarged photograph faces a page of solid black, isolating the gaze before the sequence gradually pulls back to reveal more of the surrounding scene, until individual faces dissolve once again into the crowd. The experience feels less like turning the pages of a photobook than adjusting one’s own eyesight – moving between intimacy and distance, lucidity and doubt.

Even the title resists certainty. Yousefi has little interest in describing what the book contains, preferring instead a phrase that preserves the ambiguity he found in the archive. “There are so many faces that are not sure,” he says. By the final pages, those eyes have quietly dissolved back into the crowd. What lingers is a fleeting exchange – one person behind a camera, another before it – and the quiet feeling of having briefly met someone who, in that moment, wanted to be seen.

Eyes Dazzle as They Search for the Truth is published by Luhz Press, distributed internationally by Idea Books, and available for €48,95.

items.title: Nick Haymes’s Family, Every Which Way
items.content:
Nick Haymes lived only a couple of blocks from the World Trade Center. Chronograph, published by SPBH Editions / MACK, opens on images of the catastrophe, September 11, 2001, before the subject shifts toward the family unit — intimate terrain Nick Haymes would go on exploring for twenty-five years. From there, Lina, his partner, and later their sons Philipp and Lawrence, overrun every photograph, caught in their trivial, everyday lives as much as in more solemn moments.

The father makes no attempt at the perfect shot. In his pictures, the children often have their eyes shut. A child howls with rage, his mouth full of yoghurt, rather than smiling for the camera. Drool regularly smears the chin, snot runs: in real life, children could not care less about their manners. These images, which a technical eye would call failures, never end up in the bin. Chronograph draws its strength from exactly that: the accident stands in for the truth.

The title borrows from the vocabulary of horology: a chronograph measures the passing of time, minute by minute. Chronograph works in the same register, collecting recurrences — a handful of motifs that return page after page like familiar landmarks. The same nose bleeding under a blue-tiled shower, the same bathtime ritual. One can almost imagine cohabiting within the 800 square feet of their New York apartment, in this endearing, familiar chaos.

The catalogue of small domestic accidents lengthens with every page. A grazed knee, a lost tooth brandished like a trophy, a cut finger, a splint one day, a cast scrawled with doodles the next. A nose bleeds, again, under the shower. One could almost mistake it for war… seen at a child’s height. A sole of a foot, a few warts breaking its surface, even gets its own close-up.

Lina, the children’s mother, regularly appears in frame, sometimes nude or in her underwear, sprawled across an unmade bed or a sofa, never in a studied pose. The children undress just as naturally, unbothered by the lens, alone or curled against her. This shared nakedness escapes the usual modesty of family albums: it speaks of an innocence that precedes self-consciousness, a tender and natural relationship to the body.

Between the two brothers, the camera mostly captures the disorder inherent to siblinghood: silly string flying in white filaments through a ransacked bedroom, a Jenga tower teetering, a quarrel whose shouts one can only guess at. Their father photographs them from every angle, with the same attention paid to each. This disorder also makes room for stillness: a hand resting on a shoulder, a glance seeking another in the middle of a game, never staged and all the truer for it.


Elsewhere, the book gives itself over entirely to farce. A boy bolts naked down a hotel corridor. Another is immortalized urinating in the bathroom, wearing a Mexican wrestling mask. The younger boy, also masked, devours a chocolate cupcake with both hands, his face smeared with chocolate. Blond and curly-haired, he multiplies his antics: grimaces, absurd poses, in a comic generosity all his own.

Rituals return with the same regularity as the scrapes and bruises. One of them stands apart in its gravity: death makes its first, quiet entrance into the book. The family hamster, who appears repeatedly and was often good for a laugh, seemed a full-fledged member of the household. He is buried in a small cardboard coffin, carefully made. A ceremony photographed like reportage, foreshadowing the human losses to come.

The years pass: the children grow up, the adults grow old. Childhood nakedness gives way to a new modesty. On a black-and-white beach, two young men, childhood now firmly behind them, walk bare-chested.


Toward the end of the book, illness settles in without warning on Mikhail Kutsovsky and Nadezhda Kutsovskaya, Philipp and Lawrence’s grandparents, already familiar to the reader from earlier kitchen scenes and family gatherings. They appear undergoing dialysis, hooked to IVs in beige recliners, under the wan glow of fluorescent lights. Further on, one of the boys leans over his bedridden grandmother, his hand resting tenderly on hers.

We find them again in a hospital room, before their final separation. They die a year apart, but the book reunites them one last time, at the burial. In a striking image, two urns rest side by side on a table draped in blue. Philipp and Lawrence each play an important, symbolic role in the ceremony, visibly moved. On a nearby easel stands the photograph of the grandfather holding his grandsons as children, already seen earlier in the book.

A cycle closes here. One leaves this small world reluctantly, closing the book. This family is already missed.

Chronograph by Nick Haymes is published by SPBH Editions / MACK, and is available at £55.

items.title: Inez & Vinoodh: Glamour, Desire, and Subversion
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Inez & Vinoodh: Glamour, Desire, and Subversion

The unsettling body of work by the celebrated Dutch photography duo can be seen until September 6 at Kunstmuseum Den Haag in The Hague (Netherlands), as part of the retrospective “Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh”, or in the book of the same name published by Hannibal Books.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Inez & Vinoodh.

Inez van Lamsweerde (b. 1963) and Vinoodh Matadin (b. 1961), a couple in life as in work since meeting in Amsterdam in 1986, rank among the most influential photography duos of their generation. In December 2023, they created the now-iconic portrait of Taylor Swift, named Person of the Year by Time magazine. The superstar was photographed in New York with her cat, Benjamin Button, draped over her shoulders — a pose inspired by Cat People, a 1978 book by American photographer Bill Hayward, of which Inez had given the singer a vintage copy.

From the 1990s onward, Inez & Vinoodh made their name with digitally retouched fashion photographs, a practice still rare at the time, which they explored well before the Photoshop era. Their sleek, polished aesthetic stood in sharp contrast to the documentary-style grunge look then dominant, embodied by photographers such as Juergen Teller, and found a home in publications like The Face, a cult British fashion and music magazine, and Vogue. While their work goes far beyond simple celebrity commissions, an entire room of the exhibition is devoted to their portraits of pop-culture figures, including actress Tilda Swinton, singer Billie Eilish, model Kate Moss, and singer Rosalía.

Acting as both mirror and magnifying glass, Inez & Vinoodh’s photography draws on popular culture even as it questions it. Beneath the glamour, the grotesque often surfaces, classic gender roles are upended, and an unsettling unheimlich quality — familiar yet disquieting — runs through much of their work. The “Fashion Plate” series, created during lockdown, pairs high jewelry with cut-out fashion images, for Vogue Paris.

The duo also explores nature through botanical still lifes, a practice they have pursued for several years. This strand draws on the Dutch tradition of floral still-life painting, while steering it toward a stranger kind of beauty, somewhere between elegance and oddity. It extends, beyond portraiture, their fascination with metamorphosis and the ambiguity of form.

Since 1999, the kiss has been a recurring motif in Inez & Vinoodh’s work. More than a simple gesture, it represents for them a form of total union, the point at which two people nearly cease to be distinct from one another. The exhibition brings together several works from the “Me Kissing…” series, self-portraits of the couple kissing, alongside the brand-new “Think Love” (2025) series, which shows their son Charles kissing his partner Natalie under a red veil, photographed in the Texas desert, as if wrapped in a protective cocoon.

The exhibition “Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh” is on view at Kunstmuseum Den Haag, in The Hague (Netherlands), until September 6, 2026.

The book Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh, published by Hannibal Books, is available for €69.95.
