items.title: Jérémy Lempin: No One Is Supposed to Ignore Them
items.content:
In the aisle of a supermarket in northern France, a 74-year-old man holds a package at arm’s length, turns it over to check the date, then puts it back. Léon led a team for more than 30 years without ever learning to read. It is with this scene, as ordinary as it is disquieting, that Jérémy Lempin’s project opens.

There is something of the hush of a locker room in his images. One senses restrained gestures, faces composing themselves, hands hesitating over a notice or a form. Nothing spectacular, and the photographer is the first to say so, he who once led an entirely different life: he served aboard the aircraft carrier Charles-de-Gaulle, covered Operation Serval in Mali and Operation Sangaris in the Central African Republic, and received the Médaille Militaire from the hands of French President François Hollande before trading, in 2016, his non-commissioned officer’s cap for a photojournalist’s vest. One might expect such a background to lead toward the sensational. It does not. After the horse Peyo (World Press Photo, Visa d’or 2021) and the traumatized soldiers of Aux Armes et caetera, Jérémy Lempin chose this time to photograph what cannot be seen. The photographer says as much himself, plainly: he “does not photograph the spectacular but the ordinary,” and his images “force us to look at the daily lives of these anonymous people.”

Republic

In France, illiteracy was designated a national cause in 2013, and the label has lost none of its relevance: the French Senate raised concerns again this past April, and the National Agency for the Fight Against Illiteracy (ANLCI), whose presidency passes to Yves Rousset today, September 1, has just adopted five strategic priorities for 2025-2030. Founded in 2000, the agency remains the sole body tasked with coordinating efforts across the field, associations, the ministry of education, businesses. But the battleground is shifting: the near-total move to digital administrative procedures has turned a silent handicap into a permanent obstacle. Forms are no longer filled out at a counter; they are downloaded, signed online, verified through a digital portal. Every new online procedure closes the door a little further on those who have never been able to read it.

The choice of venue for the exhibition is no accident. The Cité internationale de la langue française, a museum dedicated to the French language, occupies the château of Villers-Cotterêts, the very place where, in 1539, King Francis I signed the ordinance making French the sole language of French administration and justice, sidelining the regional languages that had coexisted until then. Nearly five centuries later, exhibiting in its courtyard the faces of those who never gained full access to that language closes a bitter loop: the founding decree of French national unity also, unintentionally, drew the outline of those it would one day leave behind.

The figures, for their part, are unambiguous: 3.7 million adults educated in France struggle with basic skills, reading, writing, arithmetic, or 10.5% of the population aged 18 to 64. One in two is employed. One in two is over 45. And 71% of them spoke only French at home at age 5, which should put to rest, once and for all, the lazy equation between illiteracy and immigration.

Since 2023, Jérémy Lempin has followed these lives in the Nord region, in Marseille, in Paris, in Bordeaux and the Charente region, and in French Guiana, an overseas territory of France in South America, six regions where, he says, the divide is “most pronounced.” What links them has less to do with statistics than with a shared reticence turned into confession: Audrey, 40, a mother of three, goes back to school so as to no longer feel helpless in the face of her sons’ homework, and says she now feels “less of that sense of embarrassment, and that’s wonderful”; Angélique, 38, half-regrets not having “worked harder at school” while there was still time. This thwarted transmission plays out again, in reverse, with Élia, 50, in Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, French Guiana: she left school at 7, and it is her daughter Éliane, top of her class with a 17-out-of-20 average in a school where 9 out of 10 students struggle badly, who teaches her French every evening. “My nine children lack for nothing,” Élia says, “but I can’t help them with their homework.” Shakel, 27, embodies the other side of the same divide: with no other way out, he once swallowed 140 cocaine pellets; a digital outreach worker today, he speaks of his time in prison with a clarity that seeks neither excuse nor effect.

Others, across mainland France, have devised their own workarounds. Alain, 47, built himself a color-coded system to navigate daily life, down to an orange cross on his wall marking the family doctor’s number; to follow a recipe, he relies on video rather than text. Joëlle, a former school cook, is relearning arithmetic as an adult: after an hour spent applying a calculation to her grocery shopping, fatigue sets in, a sign of concentration her teacher says she rarely sees elsewhere, but she comes away with unmistakable pride, that of being able to shop on her own because she can now count. Later in the book, a postcard scrawled by 12-year-old Manfred during a summer learning camp closes the loop on childhood: a few clumsy words to his mother, whose very existence measures the distance he has traveled.

French Guiana, an overseas territory of France in South America, concentrates what the rest of the country would rather ignore: nearly 40% of adults there are illiterate, 39% of men and 43% of women, and three-quarters of them are unemployed. Residents of priority urban districts and of France’s overseas territories are 2.5 times more exposed than elsewhere; in the French Antilles and on Réunion Island, the phenomenon is three times more common than in mainland France. Twenty languages are spoken there, and written French competes directly with languages commonly spoken at home. Mariam Koita, an academic officer for illiteracy prevention at the Guiana education authority, notes that for many, “even though they were born in Guiana, French is not their native language.”

The principal of Paul Jean-Louis middle school, in Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, sums up in his own way the situation at a school built for 900 students that now enrolls 1,160: “Here, if you can’t read by first grade, you’re finished.” Three knife or gun attacks took place outside the school in 2023, one of them fatal. Reading a line like that, one grasps that illiteracy is never an isolated cause: it settles into the wreckage of something else, poverty, broken families, overcrowded schools, and lodges there for good.

Reticence

This concealment is one that everyone who works with adult learners knows by heart. In the book, Cécile Montastier, a program coordinator at the Greta-CFA Aquitaine training network in France, describes the first sentences she typically hears: “I’m not capable,” “I never understood, at school,” “I’m useless.” Many, she writes, learned very early to make themselves “as small as possible,” to go unnoticed in order to avoid judgment, until that discretion became an adult reflex. Shame, more than ignorance itself, is the real obstacle: it drives people to refuse help rather than be found out, turning a temporary gap into a lasting identity.

To tell the story of this ongoing concealment, Jérémy Lempin had the almost playful idea of using a Sprocket Rocket, an analog camera sold in supermarkets, which he bought for “barely 30 euros.” “I wanted to use something familiar,” he explains, drawn to a camera whose film exposes even its own sprocket holes: “It really shows the lack of resources and awareness in these regions and among the people concerned.” Looking at a portrait taken in French Guiana in which the subject’s face disappears behind one of those holes, he adds: “I see it a bit like a ‘no entry’ sign, because they were forbidden to speak their local language when French Guiana became a French overseas department.”

The book, prefaced by French novelist Marie-Hélène Lafon, brings together 150 photographs, handwritten letters written by the people Lempin met, who thus become co-authors, and texts signed by those working on the ground: the ANLCI, the association Mots & Merveilles, and Savoirs pour Réussir. Cécile Jaffré, director of the ANLCI, writes a line in the book that could sum up the whole project: “The image reveals what is invisible.” She also points out that, unlike other obstacles, this one is reversible: “You can learn, and relearn, at any age, provided you are given the means to do so.”

The object itself makes an argument of its own. Hardcover, 264 pages, FSC- and PEFC-certified paper, the title debossed on the cover: Hemeria, a French publishing house founded in 2018, describes the book as “a timeless, universal space of expression,” an object that “can be touched, kept, shared,” in contrast to the screen. The choice is not incidental for a subject that questions our very relationship to the written word: devoting such a carefully crafted volume to illiteracy is also a way of doing justice, through form, to those long kept at a distance from books.

Ignorance of the law is no excuse, the saying goes. In every image, Jérémy Lempin reminds us that 3.7 million people are, above all, unaware that they could, at last, stop being made invisible.

L’École de la vie. Liberté. Égalité. Invisibilité. (The School of Life. Liberty. Equality. Invisibility.) is published by Hemeria on September 4, opening the French National Days of Action Against Illiteracy. The accompanying exhibition is on view at the Cité internationale de la langue française in Villers-Cotterêts until September 20. The project is screened this Wednesday evening at Visa pour l’image, in Perpignan, and exhibited during the festival.

items.title: Taylor Galloway, Home Sweet Farm
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Taylor Galloway, Home Sweet Farm

For more than a decade, Los Angeles-based photographer Taylor Galloway returned to the family farm in Hartwood, Virginia, at a time when industrial agriculture is swallowing up small farms across the United States. From that unexpected welcome came across the street from Heaven, published by Deadbeat Club.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Taylor Galloway.

An independent photographer, Taylor Galloway didn’t grow up in Virginia. Ten years ago, when he began this project, he met much of his grandmother’s family for the first time, she herself having grown up on the farm before moving away. Welcomed like one of their own, Galloway discovered there a sense of belonging he hadn’t expected. “The land has taught me everything,” he told the New York Times. “These are my people. This is where I come from.”

The images cultivate a vintage aesthetic without heavy-handed nostalgia: brown wood paneling, rotary phones, lace doilies and decorative plates, hymnals lined up side by side on a piano. Nothing here is staged for effect; everything simply seems to have stayed put, year after year, in this domestic cocoon where the beautiful and the trivial simply coexist. Most surprising of all, that reassuring familiarity doubles as a reassuring strangeness, embodied in a giant jigsaw puzzle of Bigfoot, an emblematic figure of American rural folklore, assembled with the gravity of a relic.

Among the many faces here: his grandmother, known as Gram; his great-aunt Bernice; his great-uncle Gene, who died six years before the book’s release, photographed in his kitchen alongside his dog Lulu after Sunday service; and Benjamin Dye, a fixture of the community and former starting right fielder for the 1958 Wichita Braves, photographed holding his old baseball glove. Simple, beautiful faces, strangely familiar, radiating a tenderness just beneath the skin.

The cover image, a night sky where the full moon hangs above silhouetted wildflowers, and the book’s poetic, promise-shaped title distill the project’s final intention, that of a native son come home, as in a fairy tale. According to the publisher, the book is not about “preserving the past, but about that which anchors the promise of a future, and the certainty of having found one’s way home.”

You close the book with the sense of having been given a seat at that table. And wondering whether, somewhere, you don’t have a farm of your own worth photographing.

across the street from Heaven, by Taylor Galloway, comes out in October from Deadbeat Club, with a special edition limited to 20 signed and numbered copies, including a chromogenic print and the 7″ vinyl The Hound Dog’s Hymn, a soundscape built from songs heard while working the farm.

items.title: Jean-François Leroy, Captain of Photojournalism, Dies at 69
items.content:
A former Sipa Press photographer, Jean-François Leroy served as editor-in-chief of Photo Magazine. Renowned for his editorial rigor and unwavering commitment to journalistic integrity, he was a Chevalier des Arts et Lettres and a Chevalier de l’Ordre du Mérite. Over nearly forty years, he turned Visa pour l’image into the world’s foremost gathering for photojournalism, free and open to the public, drawing more than 220,000 visitors to Perpignan every year: a platform for photographers working in the field, at odds with a news landscape he saw as increasingly driven by social media.

Just last year, for the festival’s 37th edition, he told Blind exactly why his fight still mattered: “Because the world is even more out of joint than usual, it has never needed Visa pour l’image more.” He summed up his conviction in a few simple words: “the world is in a bad way,” and the role he assigned to his profession: “journalism is a job on the front line of every piece of bad news on the planet.” He also denounced the overused word “objectivity” — “the first word we should banish from our journalistic folklore” — favoring instead a demand for honesty, and championed images “coming from the field, not from social media; images made by humans, not by [AI].”

A fellowship with photographers

That loyalty to the field also showed in the bonds Jean-François Leroy built with entire generations of photojournalists, many of whom, year after year, found their work exhibited or awarded in Perpignan.

Among them, Jean-Pierre Laffont, a longtime friend, whose decades covering the United States — where he first set foot in 1965 — were the subject of a retrospective at Visa last year. His wife Éliane and Jean-Pierre Laffont chose to share their grief upon hearing of his death, in a piece titled “Oh Captain! Our Captain!”:

“Dear Jean François, Jean Pierre and I have been your friends for 40 years, we were so young then, full of ideas, hope and ambition and with health that could withstand anything…. We could discuss photography all night and go to work in the morning without having had an hour of sleep… We did so many things together, photography festivals, books, shows… And in every corner of the planet… We also had some great laughs because you are the funniest friend I know, the most flamboyant too and the one with the biggest mouth!

You are the friend everyone should have, phenomenal, charismatic, spiritual, profound, curious, loyal, passionate and fascinating, you also have a great moral ethic and an immense sense of justice…You are the best, the greatest!

Jean François, you have changed the lives of thousands of photographers, including Jean Pierre. You are the first to have taken photojournalism out of the pages of newspapers and magazines and put it on walls, in churches, in convents, in the prisons of the city of Perpignan and I will always remember Jean-Pierre’s wonder and emotion when he saw his photos on those giant screens… Jean François, you changed the way people see the world and the way photographers see their work.

The world of photography without you is simply unimaginable. You are the captain, the lighthouse in the storm. I wish I could light up the Eiffel Tower and tell you what a beautiful light you are and that will remain in our lives.

Éliane and Jean-Pierre”

Sick, but at his post to the very end

Jean-François Leroy died Monday morning of cancer, surrounded by loved ones at his home in Paris. Despite his illness, he had taken part “from A to Z in preparing” this 38th edition, Delphine Lelu, managing director of Visa pour l’image, told the AFP news agency. “He is the soul of this festival, he carried it on his shoulders from the very first edition, in 1989. He leaves us a great legacy. He always wanted Perpignan to be a beacon for photojournalists, and we will make sure the festival keeps shining,” she added.

“The entire team of Visa pour l’image – Perpignan, and Jean-François Leroy’s whole family, are saddened to announce the death, this Monday, August 31, in the morning, of the founder and longtime director of the international photojournalism festival,” the festival announced on its Instagram account, honoring a man who “supported and showcased photojournalists from around the world.”

Axelle de Russé, a photojournalist honored several times at Visa pour l’Image for her reporting, and close to the man, also pays tribute to him, in these words: “Jean François Leroy. He wore that name so well. I think I can say that every one of us photojournalists grew up, matured, and dared, thanks to him, and to Visa pour l’Image. You come to Visa for the first time, intimidated, watching these big names from afar with admiration. Never daring to imagine that one day you might become part of that world. And then one day I got a phone call: “Axelle, it’s Jean François Leroy. You’ve won the Canon Female Photojournalist Award.” I thought it was a joke and hung up on him. We laughed about it for almost 20 years. Because we laughed with Jean François. He could be very tough, very critical of work you brought to show him. He impressed me. He had a sharp eye, an incredible talent for building a narrative. He knew how to tell stories, even the hardest ones. In 2020, I took part in what’s known as the schools’ week in Perpignan. There were 5 of us women photographers, and every day we gave middle-school classes tours of our exhibitions. I discovered a different man — funny, and generous. I don’t think I’ve ever laughed as much as I did that week. I can say it without hesitation: I am a photographer today because of him. Him, the irreverent one. He leaves us two days after the opening of the 38th edition. His tall silhouette, his slow gait, his glasses, his hat, his outbursts, his voice on the microphone, his unwavering commitment; the man embodied our profession, he was a symbol of photojournalism. We already miss him.”

The 38th edition of Visa pour l’image continues in Perpignan through September 13, 2026.

Cover image by Claude Truong-Ngoc.

items.title: Flowers of Speech
items.content:
In 1965, the poet Allen Ginsberg coined the phrase flower power to turn protest into peaceful spectacle. Two years later, photographer Bernie Boston made it an icon: a young man slipping a carnation into the barrel of a rifle at the foot of the Pentagon. Fifty-nine years have passed. The flower has not changed its name, but it has changed sides: it no longer disarms violence, it is now the object of an almost clinical suspicion. At the Jardin d’été in Arles, five artists brought together by Beata Nowak and Michel Poivert, curators of the project and authors of the book published by Textuel, no longer look to the flower for a symbol of peace. They look to it for clues.

Alice Pallot, a member of the Tendance Floue collective, followed architects Elena Seegers and Simon de Dreuille, founders of Botanical Agency, into the heart of a contradiction: floral foam, the material found in nearly every florist’s bouquet, becomes underwater “a persistent and pervasive source of pollution.” Pallot photographs the particles that break off it under horticultural LED light, invisible to the naked eye, revealed at last under a light designed to make things grow. The gesture is no laboratory accident, as the artist explains: “Bringing together scientists and artists is, for me, a way of making visible and understandable studies and articles that are sometimes impenetrable because of their inaccessible language.” After that, it is hard to look at a flower without looking at what makes it.

This same distrust of appearance drives Matei Bejenaru, who reaches back to the Brendel models, three-dimensional teaching aids made of papier-mâché, plaster, or wood, produced in Germany for the study of botany. He photographs them in color, almost like watercolors, where Karl Blossfeldt would have captured them in clinical black and white a century earlier. From a distance, the image reads as a plant. Up close, it reveals the artificiality of the replica. The doubt, for Bejenaru, is the point: it echoes a very real urgency, that of species now facing extinction.

Where Bejenaru plays on the confusion between plant and replica, Suzanne Lafont takes on a more ordinary form of blindness: the one we direct at the weeds of sidewalks, tree grates, and vacant lots. Twelve municipalities of Bordeaux Métropole on foot, plants placed on a light table to intensify their colors, then digitally inverted in reference to Goethe’s Theory of Colors. “Wild nature no longer exists,” the artist told the director of the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Bordeaux, where the work was first shown. What Lafont is fighting has a name: “plant blindness,” the cultural indifference to the vegetal world that lets us step over dozens of quiet lives every day.

The attention Lafont demands for urban weeds, Anaïs Tondeur carries even further, to the contaminated soils of the Land of Fires, near Naples, where toxic waste is buried. The plants that still grow there overproduce polyphenols, making it possible to create phytographs, chemical traces inscribed directly onto the emulsion. “Without extracting the plants from the soil, this photographic encounter takes place through nothing more than contact between the elements present,” the photographer explains. “It is one of the most environmentally respectful photographic protocols there is.” Philosopher Michael Marder then writes a letter to each plant; Tondeur reads it back to them; a second phytograph is born from that reading.

This correspondence between the human and the vegetal finds an even more intimate echo in the work of Jiang Zhi, who sets flowers alight in full bloom for his series 情书 (Love Letters), dedicated to the memory of his wife Ren Lan, whose name means “orchid” in Chinese. Ikebana, the Japanese art of embracing the ephemeral, is here subverted: the burning flower no longer seeks eternity, it sets fire to it. “The fire is as beautiful as the flower, and the flower too is entirely without flaw,” the artist says, “but of course, this is only a temporary beauty.” The flower burns. The love letter remains.

“Flower Power” runs through October 4, 2026, in the Jardin d’été, as part of the Rencontres d’Arles. Catalogue published by Textuel and available for €59.
items.excerpt: Five artists and one motif: the flower, long confined to ornament, becomes the ground for an inquiry into the living world in Arles. “Flower Power” unfolds its paper petals through October 4.

items.title: Dust and Decibels: Rave on Film
items.content:
You can feel it: these two women lived the rave from within. It was woven into their daily lives, anchored by ritual, carried by tribe. A mosaic of faces and figures caught in the grain of the film: closed eyes, a bride in a tulle veil toasting amid a circle of laughing friends, half-smiles of ecstasy wrung out at dawn while the bassline pounds on. The book stands as an ode to the great family of the free party, in all its European guises: from Italy to the Czech Republic, where CzechTek drew crowds in the thousands, by way of the Basque Country and the Provençal countryside around Aix-en-Provence.

That family, Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi first came to know separately. They crossed paths on the benches of the same art school in Milan, long before truly meeting in the mud and feedback of a wall of speakers. Both were already taking photographs, each in her own way, before finding common ground. “We had two different ways of looking at things, even though we were experiencing the same parties and were often together,” Cheyenne recalls. “One of us might be drawn to a face or a particular situation, while the other would be attracted to something completely different. And yet today, our photographs blend together perfectly.”

From this alchemy between two eyes, no individual signature remains: throughout the book, the photographers chose never to specify who took which picture. “Maybe that’s exactly the point,” Valentina suggests: “two different perspectives that, over time, became a shared memory.” A deliberate anonymity, true to the spirit of the movement it immortalises. The book is equally striking for its total absence of visual hierarchy. A wall of speakers is photographed with the same gravity as a child playing with a dog in the dust of an encampment. “It tells exactly what we experienced: situations, speakers, trucks, children, dogs and people.”

That levelling of gaze builds, page after page, into the portrait of an entire life rather than a mere nocturnal pastime. Bodies stretched out by the water, a black dog standing sentinel before a tower of speakers, whole convoys of camper vans lined up on some improvised lot. “For more than seven years, we lived on four wheels, in trucks, moving between the road and squatted social centres. Never Alone is infused with that sense of freedom and community that defined our lives,” Cheyenne and Valentina explain. The sound system here is no mere party backdrop, but an itinerant domestic architecture in which the speaker stack stands in for the hearth, the truck for the sitting room, and the road for a permanent address.

That happy nomadism, though, sits at odds with another constant running through the book, one that reads as stranger still today: the almost benevolent presence of the police. It is hard, from where we stand now, to picture a uniform ever blending into the scenery of a free party. And yet even in the rare frames where law enforcement meets the lens, no tension shows on any face. “What we experienced at the end of the 1990s can never be repeated,” they observe. “The police didn’t really know how to deal with us yet, and we were living in a time that was far less controlled than today. Now algorithms, cameras and surveillance permeate every aspect of our lives.”

Children of the Bassline

That sense of a lost innocence finds a pointed echo in the book’s foreword, written by Tobia D’Onofrio, who suggests that the children pictured here may be the very same young people now protesting against the authorities. In France, several bills aimed at further criminalising free parties are currently under consideration, following in the wake of the anti-rave decree passed by the Meloni government in late 2022. It is a lineage the photographers acknowledge without grandstanding. “Free-party culture hasn’t disappeared, and fortunately the new generations haven’t allowed themselves to be intimidated. Illegal rave parties are still being organised, less frequently and a little more under the radar, and we can only be happy about that.”

And yet this continuity, however reassuring, raises an almost vertiginous question about the photographic act itself. The American writer Hakim Bey once theorised the rave as a “temporary autonomous zone,” a gesture designed by its very nature to vanish. Photography does precisely the opposite: it arrests time, fixes it onto a light-sensitive surface. Isn’t there something paradoxical in that? The two women wave the objection away with disarming simplicity. “When we took those photographs, our intention wasn’t to ‘document’ anything. We both had a passion for photography, and for us these were simply images of our everyday lives.”

That same absence of calculation runs through their choice of medium: there is no retro affectation behind the exclusive use of black and white. “It was an editorial choice, since most of the photographs were originally shot in black and white. We have always loved black-and-white film. We also used to print the photographs ourselves in the darkroom, using an enlarger.”

Out of that artisanal darkroom labour, certain images resurface with particular force. “Every photograph brings something back and stirs something in me,” Cheyenne confides. Valentina, for her part, remembers with precision Tequinox, a party held in Bologna in 1999: “We found the location for the party only a few days before it began, thinking it was abandoned. Several sound systems arrived, along with people from all over Europe.” One senses that night in one of the book’s photographs: a square overrun with vans and huddled figures beneath a low sky, where you can almost feel the bass still trembling underfoot.

In the end, the party itself was only ever the backdrop to something larger: the wanderings of a generation in perpetual motion, for whom the collective was the answer. Few places remain today where such lives would still be possible. The free party endures as one of the last spaces of self-organised, collective and free celebration, and it is precisely for that reason that it finds itself, across Europe, in the crosshairs of politics.

All images: © Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, Courtesy of and published by DRAGO

Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, is published by Drago Propaganda, 196 pages, €60. Available at www.neveralonebook.it

items.title: A Scorching Summer in Paris, with Augustin Pasquini
items.content:
A green metal footbridge, slightly battered, over the Canal Saint-Martin. Augustin Pasquini knows it by heart, keeps coming back, has learned to spot its regulars. This is where, he says, “the light hits best.” An open-air studio set, free of charge, courtesy of a municipal decision and a heat that refuses to let up.

Summer 2026 will stay lodged in Parisian memory as the one where people stopped fleeing the city and learned to inhabit it differently, at a slower pace. Pasquini chose to stay, “for reasons of my own,” he says, almost bashfully. A lifelong Parisian, he had never seen a summer like this one. The temperature climbs, the pace collapses. “Goodbye to productivity,” he says, half-amused, half-dazed, like everyone else that summer. A floating slowness set in as early as June, an in-between state he tracked with his camera: “A gesture, a light, glistening skin.” The city, usually electric, turned humid, almost sleepwalking. Pasquini, used to capturing effervescence, had to learn to photograph waiting instead.

It was in this humidity that the eclipse arrived. Montmartre, a mid-summer afternoon, the crowd looking up, cardboard glasses strapped on. Pasquini remembers the 1999 eclipse, which he never photographed, and which had stayed with him. This time, he went with his sister. But when the moment came, he barely looked through his own glasses — he shot instead. “I did what I had to do, where I find the most meaning,” he says, true to an instinct that never fails him: stay close to the subject, even if it means missing the spectacle itself. He speaks of “a suspended moment of communion, a little strange, a little apocalyptic.” The phrase reads like an omen for the rest of the summer.

Because it was the canal that occupied the photographer, body and soul, all season long. A political decision, the legalization of swimming, and suddenly the Canal Saint-Martin changed status, changed crowd, changed skyline. “The canal belongs to everyone now,” Pasquini observes, having grown up in the neighborhood and understanding, better than anyone, the scale of the shift. “It can never go back to how it was,” he repeats, almost incredulous at the force of a simple municipal decree. One might smile at that, except the phrase happens to be true: inflatable mattresses, paddleboards, soon jet-skis too, people joke on the embankment.

The photographer settled in as a regular, a neighbor more than a hunter of images. Always with a 35mm: “I prefer to shoot everything at 35 millimeters, on Fujifilm,” a focal length that “forces you to move, to be close, present, connected, not to cheat.” On this green footbridge, he recognizes faces, greets local celebrity Hamza la douane and his friends, warns the more reckless jumpers: “Two meters fifty of depth, that’s not much.” A drunk young Englishman jumps anyway, gets hurt, comes back proud. Pasquini watches, photographs a few of the jumps, nothing more. There was also the day a man drowned in front of him, the stunned crowd, himself included, watching rescuers struggle in vain. He chose not to photograph it. Sometimes silence is worth more than a shutter click.

From this suspended summer, Pasquini says he drew a confirmation rather than a revelation — color, 35mm, a warm color palette pushed even further. “When I started sorting through my images, and I saw my closeness, and these bodies, I told myself I had something,” he confides. Not a commissioned report, not confined to his own neighborhood — the street entire, all of Paris, under a heat that reshaped bodies and habits. A practice sharpened by repetition, the calm of a photographer who now knows exactly where he needs to be on the fifteenth of August.

There remains that little tune, half fatalistic, half tender, that circulated along the quays all summer: they say this is the coolest summer of the rest of our lives. Pasquini, for his part, prefers other words, simpler ones, true to what he lived through: “This summer, my own energy, different, aligned with this city.”

More information on Augustin Pasquini on his website and his Instagram.
items.excerpt: Summer 2026 had that particular flavor: a city emptied of its certainties, slow-cooked, where a young Parisian photographer chose to stay and watch it all. Augustin Pasquini was the privileged witness of a season unlike any other.

items.title: Visa pour l’Image 2026: Reality Fights Back
items.content:
On January 6, 2026, a photograph circled the globe within hours: Nicolás Maduro, President of Venezuela, handcuffed and flanked by two American marines. The image was fake, generated by AI. In his editorial for this 38th edition, festival founder Jean-François Leroy does not soften the blow: “reputable media outlets and journalists who have been raised on social media—which they have come to regard as a source of information—were taken in.” And yet, he argues, the AI revolution “may be journalism’s best chance for survival,” since these models, to be effective, “must be fed reliable, up-to-date, and verified data.”

This tension, between the image manufactured in a single click and the one photographers go out and earn, sometimes at the cost of their lives, runs through the entire 2026 programme. Pierre Conte, president of the festival association, sets this 38th edition within a larger story: the bicentenary of the invention of photography, but also the two-hundredth anniversary of Le Figaro, the doyen of the French press, and the defiant good health of The New York Times, which, he notes, “has never had so many subscribers.” His conclusion comes down to a single sentence: “Photojournalism and the media share a common destiny.” Ten exhibitions, in particular, embody that conviction.

The icon of the craft opens the way. For the first time in thirty-eight editions, Visa devotes a retrospective to Raymond Depardon, co-founder of the Gamma agency and a longtime Magnum member: not the contemplative filmmaker the public knows by heart, but the young reporter who chased wars and palace corridors long before he learned to slow down. The exhibition “Reporter/Photographer” moves across half a century of current affairs seen at eye level, all in black-and-white film: a Christian Falangist photographed in Beirut in 1978, the elated crowd before the Brandenburg Gate on the morning of November 11, 1989, a hushed exchange between French President François Mitterrand and Socialist Party First Secretary Lionel Jospin in 1988. No drone footage, no retouching: just a man, his camera, and the decisive instant. In some sense, it is the festival’s own unspoken manifesto.

The narrative then tightens around a far harsher kind of waiting. Élise Blanchard, winner of the prestigious World Press Photo prize and now based in Nairobi, spent seven years earning the trust required to make “Afghanistan: The Girls Sold to Survive Drought”, shot in Afghanistan’s Badghis province. There, unable to afford fodder for their livestock, entire families sold their daughters into marriage — prepubescent girls, some no older than ten, exchanged for a few thousand euros. The photographer gives faces and names to this trade in misery: Bulbul, fourteen, pregnant by the 45-year-old man her father married her to; Samia, fourteen, and her sixteen-year-old husband, separated the day after their wedding as he set off to find work in Iran. Seven years spent in Kabul made this work possible, and from it she drew a chilling title, In a Taliban’s House: it took all that time for these faces to agree to be shown, and it is precisely that time which lends this work both its worth and its bitterness.

A radical shift in register follows, with the festival’s most unexpected subject. In Japan, a very real phenomenon has a name: fictosexuality, a romantic and sometimes marital attachment to fictional characters. A regular contributor to Le Figaro Magazine, Jérôme Gence followed several such figures for “Virtual marriages in Japan.” In it we meet Kondo, the groom, who leaves the chapel to applause from his guests, holding a soft toy in the likeness of Hatsune Miku, the Japanese virtual pop star. Fifty-eight-year-old Roy dines every week in a neighbourhood Italian restaurant with a doll representing the same character, a union he describes as exclusive. And Lucie, twenty-four, who has lived in Tokyo for a year, married Mami, a character from the series Rent-A-Girlfriend, in a ceremony arranged entirely by a company specializing in “2D weddings.” Beneath the anecdote that draws a smile lies a far more serious vertigo: what if the true subject of 2026 were not the fabrication of images, but our increasingly porous relationship with reality itself?

The journey needed a breath of air, and it comes from beneath the waves. A marine biologist as much as a photographer, Laurent Ballesta dives himself to compose his images. He presents “Far from the Sky”: giant devil rays gliding off La Paz, grey reef sharks circling in formation in the Fakarava lagoon, a heart-shaped anemone barely six centimetres wide clinging to a sunken pontoon crane in the Gulf of Lion. No war, no human figure in sight this time, only the raw reality of the seabed and the environmental threat looming over it. Ballesta was in fact awarded this year’s Ecology 360 Prize, a reminder that in photojournalism, beauty too is a form of information.

The thread then shifts to an India suspended outside of time. Since the 1990s, Paolo Roversi has built a visual language of blur, long exposures, and sepia tones, the polar opposite of the instant news photograph. “The Smell of India” gathers this patient body of work: a scene on the road to Pushkar in 1991, the bustle of Sardar market in Jodhpur, a young boy asleep in Calcutta in 1990. Nothing current here, but a radically different way of bearing witness: less documenting a fact than distilling a feeling.

Gerd Ludwig has documented Chernobyl for more than three decades, in colour, with “No End in Sight: Chernobyl 40 Years Later.” The choice of colour is deliberate: recognized as one of the leading colour photographers of the former USSR, Ludwig refuses to let the disaster freeze into the past, seeking instead a raw, contemporary realism. His images, taken between 1993 and 2026, follow a disaster that has never stopped mutating: workers permitted only fifteen minutes a day inside the sarcophagus, their dosimeters constantly monitored; five-year-old Veronika, hospitalized for leukemia in Kyiv; rusted cribs in an abandoned nursery in Pripyat. The exhibition runs all the way to the most recent twists — illegal returnees, disaster tourism, military occupation, and a Russian drone strike on the zone in 2026 — proof that the disaster, forty years on, still keeps making news.


Étienne Montès, for his part, covered international news on the ground from 1973 to 1987, before walking away entirely. He presents “Fifteen years of photojournalism, then stop!,” a look back at fifteen years of tragedy, danger, and camaraderie across France, Spain, Africa, and Central and South America: downtown Johannesburg in 1985, solidarity in a Chilean slum in 1987, an ice cream vendor used as a human shield during a gunfight in San Salvador in 1980. After that, Montès left photojournalism to take over his family’s vineyard at the foot of the Aspres mountains, in the Roussillon. An exit as radical as it is rare in this line of work.

In Sierra Leone and Liberia, a new synthetic drug is devastating the youth. Kush, sold at rock-bottom prices, causes rapid addiction and often fatal injuries. A Belgian photographer and member of Agence VU, known for tackling the harshest social subjects, Gaël Turine documents for “Broken by Kush” tens of thousands of young people wandering the streets of Freetown and Monrovia, their bodies and lives shattered by addiction: one man rents out his pipes to other users to fund his own habit; 39-year-old Hawa, whose three children have been placed in an orphanage, survives through prostitution in an abandoned cemetery, each client barely covering the cost of her next hit. Clandestine labs keep multiplying, the authorities remain powerless, and it is families and neighbourhood committees who are left, alone, trying to save what can still be saved.

Michael Yamashita, by contrast, chose the long view to tell the story of an economic transformation. A longtime contributor to National Geographic, for which he has shot sixteen major stories in China, forty years of work make up “East Meets West — 40 Years of Photography in China”: students at an elite private school in Guangdong returning to class after morning exercises in 1995, a man carrying styrofoam by bicycle to a recycling centre in Foshan in 1996, red chili peppers drying in the sun near the Han Dynasty Great Wall in 2002. A China caught mid-transformation.


Finally, a war that has remained almost invisible since 2023. In the highlands of Ethiopia’s Amhara region, a local nationalist militia known as Fano has launched an armed insurgency that has already seized vast territories, fuelled by the neighbouring war in Tigray and by abuses committed by government forces against civilians. Winner this year of the Camille Lepage Prize for his work in Myanmar, Robin Tutenges travelled through these rebel-held territories, cut off from the world, for “Fano’s Kingdom”: fighters gathered on the heights of the Lasta massif, former regional special forces members playing checkers with sorghum beer bottle caps, worshippers kissing a church door in prayer before battle. He embodies a generation of photographers willing to go, up close, to the conflicts the rest of the world has stopped watching.

For Jean-François Leroy, this edition cannot simply celebrate photography — it must also name its adversaries. Traditional media, he writes, are “the last bastions against the gravediggers of reality,” whether “political or technological.” Whose only dream, he says, is “to tear them down or take them over to further their own agendas—and, above all, their business interests.” He points to the deals hastily struck between newsrooms and AI giants, wondering whether they have struck “a deal with the devil, who is eager for their data.”

More bluntly still, he denounces “witch hunts disguised as taxpayer-funded investigative committees” which he accuses of being “designed to advance a freedom-destroying ideology.” Faced with all this, he offers no promise of victory, only a renewed resolve: “to stand tall, or be set straight, but always remain standing.” A phrase that holds true for the photojournalism he has defended for nearly forty years, for the festival he still carries at arm’s length, and perhaps, quietly, for himself.

The 38th edition of Visa pour l’Image runs from August 29 to September 13, 2026, in Perpignan, France. Full programme and hours at visapourlimage.com

items.title: Sheila Metzner and Lillian Bassman, Fashion by Hand
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Sheila Metzner and Lillian Bassman, Fashion by Hand


In Paris, La Galerie Rouge brings together two towering American fashion photographers whose prints turned advertising commissions into pictorial gestures.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Sheila Metzner.

Lillian Bassman and Sheila Metzner were both born in Brooklyn, the former in 1917, the latter in 1939. Both also spent time as art directors before turning to photography. Between 1945 and 1948, Lillian Bassman ran the magazine Junior Bazaar, where she championed young photographers soon to become legends, Richard Avedon foremost among them. Sheila Metzner became, in 1966, the first female art director at the advertising agency Doyle Dane Bernbach. Lillian Bassman turned to fashion photography as early as the late 1940s, working in black and white for Harper’s Bazaar; Sheila Metzner, self-taught, came to it a generation later, working in color, before becoming, in 1981, the first woman bound to Vogue by an exclusive contract.

It is in the darkroom that their styles diverge most sharply. Lillian Bassman veiled her negatives in fabric and ferrocyanide until her models’ dresses became little more than the suggestion of a garment. Richard Avedon once said of her: “It’s magical what she does. No one else in the history of photography has made visible that heart-breaking invisible place between the appearance and the disappearance of things.” Sheila Metzner, by contrast, entrusts her negatives to the Atelier Fresson, whose process, perfected in 1952, demands two to three weeks of handcrafted labor to yield the richness of color and the golden glaze that lend her images the air of paintings.

Sheila Metzner borrows far more from cinema than mere light. She sketches storyboards before every shoot and hired, as a collaborator, cinematographer Peter Sova, who taught her to use HMI lighting, a technique that mimics daylight and which she has favored ever since over strobe or flash. For her first Vogue commission, photographing Parisian haute couture, she had to work at night, since clients occupied the clothes by day.

Editorial assignments gave Sheila Metzner a freedom fashion alone could not always offer. They led her, among other places, to the Samburu and the Maasai, two pastoral peoples of East Africa she describes as living gods, so struck was she by their bond with nature, a largely unseen chapter of her work. Lillian Bassman found that same freedom in her own way: withdrawn from the industry by the late 1960s, she rediscovered, in the early 1990s, negatives she had believed lost, and went on reinterpreting them until her death in 2012. Sheila Metzner’s own series, “From Life”, from which the tulips shown here are drawn, was more recently revisited at the Getty Center in 2023.

Sheila Metzner credits beauty with a “transforming power,” a conviction that runs through her entire body of work, commercial commissions included. It is this same faith in the print as a space of grace that La Galerie Rouge sets against Lillian Bassman’s, bringing the two photographers together under one roof for the first time.

 

The exhibition “C’est Chic! Sheila Metzner & Lillian Bassman” is on view at La Galerie Rouge, Paris (4th arrondissement), through September 26, 2026.

items.title: Inside John Baer’s Boxes, a Liberated Europe and a Triumphant America
items.content:
On his 25th birthday, May 7, 1945, Germany surrenders. John Baer, a journalism student at Penn State turned officer with the 644th Tank Destroyer Battalion, had landed in Normandy, fought in the Battle of the Bulge, and witnessed firsthand the horror of a Nazi concentration camp. Defeated Germany becomes, for a time, occupied territory.

“So many American soldiers wanted souvenirs, cigars and booze, Nazi flags and Lugers,” writes essayist Alexa Dilworth. He would come home with a camera instead, taken from a captured German soldier. “That John Baer claimed a Leica as a means of interacting with others and the world… is significant.” The camera, a Model III made in 1938, would never leave his side.

As chance would have it, his battalion was then stationed in Wetzlar, historic home of the Leica company, where he took his very first photographs: a sergeant hunched over his typewriter, drafting the battalion’s reports; soldiers playing a game of ball near a farmhouse, watched by young girls whose fathers may have fought these same men.

In 1950, with his wife Louise Fuoss, he set off again for Europe. The couple settled in Montpellier and traveled through France, Spain, Germany, and Italy for nearly a year. John Baer photographed the communist posters urging American troops to leave, children playing at war with wooden guns in Franco’s Spain, the still-visible scars of a continent tending its wounds.

At the corner of Rue de la Méditerranée, Rue du Pont de Lattes, and Quai de Sauvage, he captured the crumbling façade of the O!Kay Bar, wrapped in winter mist, a stray dog crossing the frame in the foreground like an inadvertent signature. This image is one of five photographs his son, Andrew Baer, names today among his favorites in the book.

Back in New York by the summer of 1951, John Baer found work as a copywriter at a public relations firm in Midtown. By day, he wrote press releases; by night and on weekends, he walked the city, developed his negatives, and printed his photographs in the bathroom of their apartment at 215 Second Avenue, in the East Village.

An air of optimism and abundance hung over Manhattan then, and John Baer captured its quiet signs: nuns laden with shopping bags in Midtown, an elegant figure draped in a pale coat crossing the sidewalk in front of a shopfront. Not far off, on a bench in Bryant Park, one man dozes between another seated with clasped hands and a third absorbed in his newspaper, while in the foreground a passerby’s leg slices through the frame: a snapshot he would title Passing Time.

From the fifth-floor apartment, the fire escape became his ideal vantage point, framing the comings and goings of the street below. Elsewhere in the city, at the corner of Lexington Avenue and 41st Street, he caught the reflection of a pedestrian beneath an umbrella, doubled in a puddle, Rainy Day Reflections.

The most ambitious series of this period remains the one devoted to the pavers of Fifth Avenue, engulfed in clouds of asphalt steam, reduced to charcoal-dark silhouettes. This rigor found its consecration in 1953: John Baer and his college friend Barney Weinberg became the first non-painters exhibited at the Abingdon Square Painters gallery, a West Village collective. He mounted unframed photographs on large horizontal panels, composing contrasts that read like frames from an experimental film.

In those same years, he pushed the experimentation even further, cutting up some of his own prints by hand with a blade, inverting black and white, reassembling silhouettes of skaters and boxers, an entirely manual process, an analog forerunner of what would, much later, become digital retouching. This is the height of his practice, one already nearing its end.

“Most of John’s work as a photographer was boxed up by 1956, when I was four,” recalls Andrew Baer. No single event seems to explain the stop. His energy simply found other outlets: “He continued to exercise his curiosity through organic gardening, ordering unusual seeds and sprouting them in window boxes; cooking Asian recipes that called for exotic spices; and campaigning for the environment,” his son explains. “As a father he was supportive, playing baseball and fishing with me and my brother Joe. Later, when I rebelled against cultural norms, he was sympathetic to my causes.

A few prints nonetheless followed Andrew Baer through his own moves over the years, including the long-admired Fifth Avenue pavers. But it would take until 2021, in the middle of the pandemic, for him and his wife, Megan Moynihan, to finally turn to the full archive that had stayed sealed for decades: more than 4,000 negatives, contact sheets, and silver gelatin prints. “John’s prints made us realize that there could be something special buried in the negatives, contact sheets, and notebooks,” Andrew Baer remembers, “but we didn’t really have any idea of how to investigate the jumbled collection.”

The turning point came when they sent a few scans to Steve Smith, a photography professor at the Rhode Island School of Design, who rushed over almost immediately: “His early validation of John’s work made us realize that the prints were just the tip of the iceberg.” Three years of digitizing later, they reached out to art director Yolanda Cuomo, known for her work with Magnum Photos. Her reply came at once: “Beautiful photos! Let’s meet.”

What strikes Andrew Baer most, looking back over it all, is not the war or the streets of Paris, but the formal daring of his father’s final years: the abstract shadows of Stuyvesant Town, the figures suspended on the ice at the Rockefeller Center skating rink. “His pictures escape the gravity of the real to become something else, something stylized and symbolic,” writes Alexa Dilworth in the essay that closes the book.

“The Leica III has a small viewfinder, no light meter, nothing is automatic. And watching John take pictures, even of my children, was watching a craftsman apply his trade,” Andrew Baer says. He had the camera serviced by a specialist repairman, cleaned, lubricated, adjusted. Through him, the Leica keeps framing the world.

John Baer, The Extraordinary Ordinary: A Memoir in Photographs, 1945–1954, published by the John Baer Archive, edited by Andrew Baer and Megan Moynihan, with an essay by Alexa Dilworth. 248 pages, $65.

An exhibition of forty prints and a book launch will be held at White Loft, 273 Grand Street, 2nd floor, New York, September 17–19, 2026. Opening reception and panel discussion Thursday, September 17, from 5 pm (talk at 6:30 pm), with Andrew Baer, Megan Moynihan, Yolanda Cuomo, Alexa Dilworth, and Jonno Rattman, followed by a book signing.

items.title: Reds & Blues: Romain Coudrier Takes to the Road to Question America’s Malaise
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Reds & Blues: Romain Coudrier Takes to the Road to Question America's Malaise

In 2025, French photographer Romain Coudrier hitchhiked 1,000 kilometres across the American Bible Belt, from Selma to Chicago, to examine the country’s polarization through a red-and-blue duotone that gives the series its title, “Reds & Blues.”

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Romain Coudrier. 

Nothing destined Romain Coudrier to cross this belt of states, an evangelical Protestant country where the church and the gun shop often share the same parking lot. In 2025, he travels to Selma, Alabama, to present his series “Bifröst,” devoted to the landscapes of Norway’s Far North, awarded at the Nuits Photographiques de Pierrevert. The work is exhibited for a week in Selma. From there, he could have gone home. Instead, he extends his stay by two weeks to visit a friend in Chicago. “A good pretext to meet Americans on the road,” he sums up.

Hitchhiking is no accident of circumstance. It is a working method he has practiced for years, already tested during the nine months of “Heimat,” on the roads of Europe, within the tradition of gonzo photojournalism, where the aim is to “let [his] own experience become the very material of the narrative.” An American myth he wanted to test, he says, “by dismantling [his] own preconceived ideas, inherited from certain beatnik books.”

On the road, every driver who stops becomes a potential subject. He photographs those who pick him up, but also motel clerks, waiters, and homeless people met along the way, “as long as there’s a connection,” he specifies. On the protocol for these portraits, the rule is clear. “There’s no negotiation. I explain what I’m doing, I ask, it’s yes or no, and that’s that. Usually, it’s yes,” he adds. “I had few disappointments, only with people I hadn’t asked.”

The series’ colour scheme reflects a precise geography: heading north from the south, from red states, presumed to lean Republican, to blue states, voting Democrat, this choice mirrors the political drift of the territory crossed. “I wanted to build an evolution from the beginning to the end of the series, and this duotone quickly imposed itself,” he explains. Once on the ground, this pattern confronts him everywhere, from sports jerseys to fast-food straws: “It became an obsession.” The introspective arc of the journey, from tension to a more bitter disillusionment, ultimately fixes the palette of his prints into “piss red” and “gas blue.”

Almost from the first mile, Romain Coudrier is branded by those he meets as an outsider, which in this context means unwelcome, even dangerous. “So my first encounter is with other people’s fear, a fear that was surprising at first, then wearing, and which ended up weighing on me,” he confides. “I’m met with very different looks and postures depending on whether I’m buying a sandwich at the register or approaching someone filling up their tank. Yet I have the same backpack, the same raincoat, the same unmistakable accent.”

As for the criminal imagery running through the series, he admits to an initial ignorance. “That’s quite foreign to me,” he concedes, regarding well-known figures of American road crime, before coming to grasp how much this imagery, dated but still very much alive, serves daily as an alibi for refusal. Hence the inclusion of police reports, court files, and local press clippings, mixed with objects gathered along the road.

“Reds & Blues” passes no verdict. “This isn’t a critique of individuals, but an observation of how a structure shapes individuals,” he insists. “Conformism is never far off, and it’s easy to moralize from behind a camera.” The series, he clarifies, “isn’t an anti-American series: it questions a social bond that is conditioned, even damaged, by mechanisms that go beyond nationality or belief.”

The hardest thing to reconcile plays out within himself, in what he calls a bourgeois-bohemian relationship to the road: “I show up, I talk, I listen, I go back to my world.” He meets people from every social class along the way, some of them in situations of extreme precarity, with whom a chance misunderstanding may have confused him, himself standing roadside with his own sign. “The series is dedicated to them.”

items.title: Joel-Peter Witkin: “Everyone Is a Freak”
items.content:
You don’t walk into a Witkin show without a shiver. From his studio in Albuquerque, New Mexico, the photographer, born in Brooklyn in 1939, has built a body of work that this California exhibition gathers in its most celebrated images, alongside rarer prints, tracing the arc of a career that resists easy categories.

The Raft of George W. Bush (NM, 2006) offers the most audacious proof of it. Witkin hijacks Géricault’s famous Raft of the Medusa to set adrift the former president, his mother Barbara, along with Condoleezza Rice, then Secretary of State, former Vice President Dick Cheney, and Colin Powell, a former Secretary of State, caught in comic and unflattering poses. The artist calls it “a contemporary ‘Ship of Fools,'” in which an angel “holds a large bone signifying cannibalistic capitalism, that charnel house of our dismal social progress.”

Beneath the provocateur lurks a relentless worker. Before photographing bodies, Joel-Peter Witkin served as a photographer in the US Army. Armed with formidable academic credentials, a double master’s degree in arts and fine arts, he brings an almost architectural attention to matter itself. Each image is born of a deliberately unhurried process. For his compositions, the artist builds entire studio scenes from painted backdrops, symbolic props, and meticulously choreographed figures, in the lineage of the great Spanish masters of painting: Goya, Velázquez, and Picasso.

This devotion to decorum carries through in his stubborn refusal of digital retouching. Witkin, who works exclusively on film, prefers to subject his negatives and prints to intense physical manipulation, scratching, tearing, bleaching, encaustic, hand-drawing, hand-tinting, giving his images a dense texture that sits somewhere between photograph and painting. Collage, another of his obsessions, conjures a cubist face out of a tangle of materials in Picasso In Purgatory (NM, 2015), as if pulled from a dream.

Humor is rarely absent. In Witkin’s hands, it flirts with sacrilege. Hitler Posing with The Anti-Christ, 1937 (Maquette, NM, 2015) is further proof, blending the grotesque and history with a nonchalance that never excludes gravity. It’s this pairing that gives his work its particular tension, where laughter arrives a beat before unease reclaims its ground.

His subversive still lifes, populated with singular bodies arranged in poses borrowed from classical painting, aren’t after cheap provocation, he insists. “I’ve always hated the term ‘freak show’ because everyone is a freak,” Witkin once declared in a speech at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. The photographer selects his models, whom he recruits through classified ads or chance encounters, with an almost clerical rigor, seeking out beings that nature has singled out and elevating them to the rank of pictorial subjects, as in Studio of the Painter (Courbet), Paris, 1990, or The Graces, LA, 1988.

“We’re on earth because we all must overcome our spiritual, mental, and physical; by ‘unselfish’ love, and by the faith that we’re really citizens of another world — of Heaven,” Witkin continued, a man who, early on, had set out to paint God. That faith surfaces in Nature Sees the First Human Death, Mexico, 2017, and in Christ Dismissing The Fashionable Artists From The Temple of Art, NN, 2017, where religion, mythology, and death keep returning without ever becoming mere set dressing.

The marginalized bodies he stages upend received ideas about normalcy, holiness, and representation. Attraction and repulsion hold each other in precarious balance, an equilibrium found again in Imperfect Thirst (NM, 2016) and The Soul Has No Gender (Mexico, 2016), two portraits in which the ambiguity of gender and identity takes on poetic form.

Long since held in the collections of MoMA, the Centre Pompidou and the Met, his photographs have lost none of their capacity to unsettle. Joel-Peter Witkin will also be inducted into the International Photography Hall of Fame in 2026, where he will receive the Visionary Award.

That may be the artist’s real feat: building a body of work embraced by institutions while still resisting consensus. In Los Angeles this summer, it still bites.

“Joel-Peter Witkin: Selected Works 1973-2018” runs through September 26, 2026 at the Fahey/Klein Gallery, in Los Angeles.
items.excerpt: Since the 1970s, the American photographer has been building living tableaux where art history collides with religious iconography, satire with the sacred, the powerful with the damned. Fahey/Klein Gallery in Los Angeles now devotes a retrospective to his work.

items.title: From Calotype to Pixel: 200 Years of Scottish Photography
items.content:
IN IMAGES

From Calotype to Pixel: 200 Years of Scottish Photography

Like this shot by Wendy McMurdo, Scottish photography has never stopped tampering with reality, the better to tell its country’s story. This summer, Dalkeith Palace, the historic seat of the Dukes of Buccleuch on the edge of Edinburgh, traces two centuries of the medium, from the pioneering calotypes of Hill & Adamson to today’s documentary practice, marking the bicentenary of the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA). A photographer-by-photographer tour of the show.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos: courtesy of PhotoDalkeith RSA200

Standing before his own paintings of tulips, Derrick Guild paints decorative patterns directly onto living tulips. Follower documents this performance, given at the RSA’s Annual Exhibition in 2016, in which the artist takes on the role of a follower of the Dutch Golden Age. The scene replays tulip mania, when a single flower could fetch ten times a skilled craftsman’s annual wage. Trained at Duncan of Jordanstone College of Art and Design in Dundee, Derrick Guild has since painted still lifes haunted by the Flemish and Dutch masters.

Daniel Cook immerses himself in the lives of his subjects for a practice that is at once documentary and fictional, giving voice to communities whose stories are too often left untold. Ricky Babes belongs to his series “Love Letters From Aberdeenshire”. Winner of the RSA’s Morton Award in 2019, he lives and works in Glasgow.

A fragment of nature, ribboned with blades of grass and a spider’s web, rendered almost abstract by the close-up. Matthew Dalziel and Louise Scullion have worked in collaboration since 1993, sculpting, filming and photographing a nature in flux. Their installation Migrator, created in 1997 for Heathrow Airport, remains one of their best-known public commissions. The duo write that they seek to “sensually reconnect the human body to the elemental earth.”

The artist’s painted face, somewhere between self-portrait and masquerade, embodies this Self Portrait Of Us All as the Devil. Graham Fagen represented Scotland at the Venice Biennale in 2015 with The Slave’s Lament, a video installation combining a poem by Robert Burns with the voice of reggae singer Ghetto Priest. Slavery, musical influence, the symbolic power of flowers: his works, often developed over long stretches of time with other collaborators, relentlessly probe national and personal identity.

A churning expanse of water, caught mid-storm, blurs the line between sky and sea. Since 1984, Thomas Joshua Cooper has been tracing Scottish rivers back to their source, from stream to river. Born in San Francisco in 1946, he settled in Scotland in 1982 to found Europe’s first fine art photography department, at the Glasgow School of Art, and photographs with an 1898 camera, one single exposure per site, never two. “Scattered Waters”, which includes this print of the Forth, was his foundational body of work, the one that bound him to his adopted country. He became the first photographer elected to the RSA, in 2007.

A pink Venus, built from chest-of-drawers and seashells, fixes her hair before a round mirror. Calum Colvin paints onto everyday objects before photographing them, reconstructing in three dimensions the paintings of Titian, and elsewhere in the series, of Rubens, Etty, David Scott or Canova. Trained as a sculptor before completing a master’s in photography at the Royal College of Art in London, he counts Venus Anadyomene among the last prints he made using traditional colour film rather than digital.

A night sky streaked with star trails hangs over a yellow glow on the horizon. In 2002, Philip Braham bought a 6x9cm Fujifilm camera to photograph landscapes at night by the light of the full moon, itself a delayed reflection of the sun. Each print in the “Different Histories of Light” series records a precise place and time, while the long exposure also captures those star trails, deep time slipped into a single instant. A graduate of Duncan of Jordanstone, he received the RSA’s Morton Award in 2009.

Three pears sit on a white compote dish, ringed by stains and splashes of black. Nature Morte is a polymer photogravure: a positive repainted in gouache and then exposed onto a light-sensitive plate, tipping a classical, minimalist composition into abstraction. Born in Selkirk, in the Scottish Borders, Alfons Bytautas trained in Edinburgh before studying under Stanley William Hayter, the British printmaker whose Paris workshop, Atelier 17, shaped generations of modern artists. He went on to run Edinburgh Printmakers’ workshop for thirty years.

A wall of stacked stones catches fire against the fading light of the Hebrides. In 1991, Julie Brook moved alone into a natural rock arch on the uninhabited west coast of the Isle of Jura. Out of that solitude came her “Firestacks”, cairns she sets alight as the tide comes in, until the water topples them. Drawing, painting and photography extend these fleeting encounters, making them accessible to audiences beyond the site itself. She now lives on the Isle of Skye.

An eight-year-old girl poses, solemn, gazing sideways. Lady Constance Anne Montagu Douglas Scott (d. 1970), daughter of the 6th Duke and Duchess of Buccleuch, was photographed thus around 1885. She would marry the Honourable Douglas Halyburton Cairns in 1908. The portrait, drawn from the Buccleuch Collection, opens onto two centuries of family archives still kept at Dalkeith itself.

Maple leaves, captured in black and white, stand out against a dark ground. Norman McBeath photographs what he calls “the fog of the familiar,” the way habit can veil our view of well-known surroundings. In an ordinary garden, he searches for the detail that jolts the eye awake. A photographer and printmaker trained in psychology, he lives in Edinburgh and has collaborated with the Irish poet Paul Muldoon, a Pulitzer Prize winner, and the British novelist Jeanette Winterson, author of Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit.

Panels of linen, printed with ruins and beaded with embroidery, hang from a wooden rod. Leena Nammari, a Palestinian artist based in Scotland, worked for years as a nurse before training in printmaking at Duncan of Jordanstone. …it can only be here… combines photography and textile printing to speak of exile and attachment to place, weaving identity and community engagement into a single thread.

Three rocky pinnacles rise against a streaked sky, captured through a process a century and a half old. Alex Boyd climbs Scottish summits with a Victorian camera on his back and develops his wet-plate collodion negatives on the spot, wedged between rocks. This is how he photographed the Storr, an iconic rock formation on the Isle of Skye, in 2013. The print entered the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA) collections that same year, a gift from the artist, who also served as the Academy’s artist in residence on the Cuillin, the island’s other great mountain range.

Under the fluorescent strip lights of a gymnasium, a forest seems to have sprung up between the court markings. Trained as a painter, Wendy McMurdo became one of the pioneers of digital retouching, well before Photoshop existed. The Games Hall stages this confusion between technology, imagination and reality. In 2018, the Royal Photographic Society named her among its Hundred Heroines of photography.


“PhotoDalkeith RSA200” runs at Dalkeith Palace, Dalkeith Country Park, roughly twenty minutes from central Edinburgh, from 22 August to 27 September 2026 (Friday to Sunday, 10am-4pm), admission £3.

items.title: Water Without the Horizon
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Water Without the Horizon

In A Perfect Medium, published by MW Editions, physician and cell biologist Bob Farese, Jr. photographs water in all its guises, and from so close that the viewer dissolves into it, losing all sense of scale, space, and time.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Bob Farese, Jr.

After air, water is perhaps the element that most resists photography. Elusive by nature, it is typically captured underwater, at sporting events (surfing, sailing), or on expeditions at sea. More often still, it is photographed from the shore or the deck of a boat, relying on the horizon to give it context and composition for, as Farese observes in his foreword, “humans tend to think of water as something outside ourselves.”

By removing that horizon line, the photographer removes every point of reference. A burst of foam becomes its own architecture. An Icelandic glacier reveals a texture akin to charcoal shading. A school of fish takes on the grain of woven cloth. Information exists, but it is pared down to the essential and relegated to the back of the book, with the precision of a lab notebook: place, hour, date. 

Between 2020 and 2025, Farese photographed whatever water lay before him, sometimes in Paris on a November evening, sometimes in Copenhagen at dawn, sometimes at the Monterey Bay Aquarium. There is no feat of daring in these images, no waiting on the photographer’s part for the perfect wave.

This choice finds its explanation in Farese’s own path, a physician and cell biologist who studies metabolism. “I am drawn to the water that flows within us,” he writes. “We are, in essence, water. About 70 percent of our mass, but more than 99 percent of our molecules, are water.”

Medium, the title of his book, names both the vital element and the photographic support: an echo of the title of his first book, Am I Not Light, likewise borrowed from physics.

Page by page, contemplation tips over into argument. “To pollute water is to pollute ourselves,” the author affirms. “To poison water is to poison ourselves. So the simple truth is this: to care for water is to care for ourselves.” If the horizon has vanished from these images, it is also so that we might stop looking at water from a distance.


A Perfect Medium by Bob Farese, Jr., MW Editions, 144 pages, $50.
